the case of Sir Walter's Bill does not turn upon tbrift,bot upon income. All persons of 64 years of age whose incomes are less than ten shilling a week, would be entitled to a pension varying ac- cording to the amowit of their income. In no case will the pension emoted five shillings a week. The fund out of which the pensions are to be paid is to be raised by a.county rate,divided between owners and occupiers, and administered by the County Council. The Bill is open to most of the objections to which Mr. Bartley's Bill is open, and, disguise it as one may,the County Council would be converted into a rival poor-law board, and would require an enormousincrease of machinery tor adjudicating upon the pensions and preventing fraud; and there is no prospect that the fall in thti poor rates would be equal to the pension rate.

The new ball which the Wesleyans propose' to erect in Bermondsey is intended as a centre of mis- Mon enterprise for the south of London. This dis- trict is rich in associations 'of John Wesley, who was instrumental in building a chapel in it which still stands, and is devoted to missionary work by the London City Mission.. It is interesting to note that. those wilt) are about to build the new hall are retaining the most characteristic feature of the old chapel, whfch was eight-sided in ahape, a peculiar- ity the ball will reproduce, but, of course, upon a much'greaterscale. The little chapel served its purposes in its time, bat it could no longer be adapted to the much-extended needs and operations of the Wesleyan body in the Bermondsey quarter Including the cost of the site, it is believed that the outlay will not be far abort of ..£40,000.
THE CASR VALUE- OF A WORKING-

A working-man in good health and in regular employ- ment is a capitalist. His health is his capital, for while his strength is maintained he should as an artisan earn about 4 per cent, interest on £2,000 every year. Depart- ing strength means hie stock de )reciating in value. In- stead of weekly dividenOs being received,there are losses in the shape of doctors' bills. Mr. Howell, 64, Norfolk- street, Skerton (says the "Lancaster Guardian"), is a little over thirty, strongly built, of average height, with broad shoulders, as if accustomed to hard work. Be told a highly interesting story. Up to three years ago he was employed at the Lancaster Waggon Works as a " holder-up " for the strikers in the smiths' department of that busy firm, and as such was a member of the Boilermakers' Society. " And what caused you to have to give up that em- ployment ? " queried the scribe, knowing that Mr Howell was now employed IN LORD ASHTON'S LINOLEITINIFACTORY. " That's what I'm going to tell you," was the answer, "In February, 1895, I was suddenly taken ill at ths Waggon Works. I managed to get home at dinner time but could not stir out again. I did not know what was the matter and sent for the doctor. He told me that I had got rheumatic fever. I was attended medically for a month, but felt that I was getting weaker with living on milk and soda water, and thought I would like to go to the Lancaster Infirmary. My doctors agreed that I had best go there. For four months I was in the Infir- mary, and was then sent to Devonshire Hospital, Bux- ton. I came back and thou ght:to try lighter work until I regained my strength. The pain however got a lot worse, and ultimately confined me to the house. I could not walk at all. My limbs were painted with a lotion and enclosed in wadding, but this brought very little relief, the pain having become acute. I was taken to the Infirmary again, to await a vacancy in the Buxton Hospital, whithr I went for the second time on September 23rd, 1896. I was put under the baths treatment again, and was discharged nn October 14th, 1896. They gave me a card to describe my condition when I had been at home a little while, and I was sorry to have to write 'not cured.' I tried my best to follow my employment, but it was a case of " one day on and two off,' until I began to despair. 1 th,llght I was never going to get better, but one day my mother read a paragraph from a Lan- caster paper about a cure by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People and she urged me to try them. The first box did not make any difference with me, but I tried another ; I then felt an improvement. I took in all six boxes of the pills,by which time the pain had departed. Another box was taken as a finishing touch,' but I al- ready felt a new man. This was over fifteen months ago. I have not felt any pain since, and thus, having got nearly through two winters, I consider my Cure a permanent one. I used to suffer terribly on change of the weather. I Slcerton my case is well-known, and I have recommended the pills to many who have been nreatly benefited by them. Dr. Williams' Pink pin. have done for me what everything else failed to do. I weigh 12it. /Das. During my illness I had been reduced to /lit. The interviewer thoroughly satisfied himself that these statements were perfectly genuine and free from ex- aggeratinn. Instead of going down town he had gone to his room. She was so rnal that she wouldn't speak to him for a week.

div.p: When Dr. Jameson and his fellow raiders were sent to prison in this country for their armed in- vasion of the Transvaal, a petition was at once set afoot to have them treated as first-class misdemea- nants. Among the earliest to sign the memorial,as Mr. Devitt informed the House of Commons on Mon- day night, were Mr. Dillon and himself, both of whom, it is needless to remind readers, have them- selves had a bitter experience of the rigours of ordinary gaol life. A characteristic feature of Mr. Davitt's powerful speech was the instinctive re- serve which prompted him to throw into imper- sonal form a description of prison hardships obvi- ously drawn from experience. His moderate yet eloquent appeal for the infusion of a little more humanity into our prison system made a deep im- pression.

Mrs. Delia Parnell bad many heartaches and dis- appointments before, meeting her tragic death by fire. The most poignant of her trials were the fading away of a brilliant daughter and the melan- choly fate of an eminent son. It was a minor blow that her own fortune, which was once substantial, drained through her fingers; yet it was a serious matter for both herself and the family of,which she was the head tbag she sh3uld have comedown tn comparative poverty. The Parnells were'never rich. Avondale is only a small estate, though the ances- tral home of a distinguished line, and the expenses which fell upon Mr. C. S. Parnell before Irish America came to the rescue placed his property under obligations which he seems not to have re- moved. He was a born political leader, but either understood or cared little for economy. Mrs. Delia Parnell had possessions in the United States, accru- ing to her BO doubt from her parents, and from this source she maintained a social position for herself and her daughters, spending an occasional season in Paris. But she met with one business disaster after another,and the result was an old age of very strait- ened means. •

The clerks of the House of Commons, who have mina recently into public prominence fr)m a re- fusal to put vestiona of members relating to for- eign affairs on the notice paper are the three gen- tlemen who sit in wigs and silk gowns at the table of the House of Commons immediately before the Speaker's chair. Sir Reginald Palgrave, the Clerk of the House, who is supported by two clerks assis- tants, who sit on his left hand,is a great depository of constitutional and historic lore. He is one of the most eminent arclgreologists of his time,and has placed beyond a doubt by his researches the exact spots in Westminster Abbey occupied by Charles I. at his trial and the Earl of Strafford on his attain- der Sir Reginald is closely shaven, somewhat slender in frame,with large dark eyes,and very pal- lid features. He comes of a highly intellectual stock,his father was the eminent historian of the Norman peried,one of his brothers was Professor of Poetry at Oxford and the editor of the "Golden Treasury," and another the far-famed Eastern scholar.

Mr. Archibald Milman, the Clerk Assistant, is a tall, dark man with sable silver hair and somewhat stooping frame, in the sixties. He is a son of the former well-known pan of St. Paul's Cathedral. Mr. Milman is an accomplished constitutional lawyer and bistorian,with an encylericedic memory. The statement submitted by him to the Select Com- mittee on Vacating Seats takes a high place among the most valuable documents expository of consti- tutional practice.

--- Lord William NevilL has been removed to Park- hurst Prison in the Isle of Wight, which is the home cf more delicate convicts, and of which Mrs. Maybrick is an inmate. A new governor has just been appointed to the prison in the person of Major Dundas.who recently married Lady Mary Bertie, a daughter of Lord Lindsey. At Parkhurst, Lord William will be employed in the making of sacks, which means comparatively easy stitching.

The members of the Automobile Club, are whip- ping up their friends for a great motor-car demon- stration during the Easter holidays. Sixty or seventy members of the club are owners of motor carriages, and the majority of these will take Dart in it if the weather is favourable. It is a matter of business with them as well as pleasure, for, a large number of members are manufacturers, or in- terested in the manufacture of such vehicles, and they have, therefore, strong inducements to take a part in the procession. There will be no question of a racing competition, which would involve a breach of the law. All the best known types of vehicles will be represented in the orderly pleasure excursion.

The great number of female teachers in the em- ployment of the London School Board has led to a movement—not among them, but on the part of a powerful association of women interested in the progress and comfort of their sex—for the appoint- ment of a woman doctor on the staff of the hoard. This idea seems to have startled the board, who have had it under consideration for an unusually i protracted length of time; but t the pill is a bitter one to some of the older-fashioned members, they had better make up their mind to do handsomely, and with a good grace, what some other board will one day do. The principle has been admitted by the London County Couricil,who have for some time had a medical lady as an inspector of boarded-out children, and have just appointed a colleague to assist her in her duties. Sooner or later the school Board will drop into line and the heavens will not fall.

div.head: CHAPTER XXV.
div.p: CHAPTER XXV.

In a street leading south from Piccadilly Richard Musgrove carried on business as a wine merchant. He rented the ground-floor, which consisted of a shop and two small back rooms, and also the cellars. In the latter he stored wines of doubtful quality. His was not a prosperous busi- ness, Richard Musgrove being the last man capable of building up a connection. Chance customers had no inducements to continue dealing with him, his wines being occasionally undrinkable, though uniformly high-priced. Latterly his "place," as he was wont to designate his shop and the adjoin- ing rooms, had been frequented by a few men who required a rendezvous in that particular neighbour- hood, and who were willing to make it worth his while to give them a general invitation to "drop in" when they liked. It was the evening after the first hearing of Gwendoline Treherne's case before the magistrates. Musgrove stood leaning against the dusty mantel- piece of his living-room, eyeing with some impatience a frugal supper of cold beef, pickles and American cheese. The cloth was crumpled, and the knives and forks were placed haphazard on the table.

But Musgrove was not of a fastidious nature, and the general air of slovenliness did not annoy him. "I shan't wait more than five minutes longer," he exclaimed angrily. "Why the deuce can't she be punctual! But she never thinks of anyone but herself. She always was a selfish girl, and--" He stopped suddenly, and opened the door lead- ing to the shop. "That's her fumbling at the bell, I do believe." he muttered to himself more cheerfully, and hastening to the door opened it with alacrity. "I've been waiting outside a good ten minutes in the rain. Why' can't you have your bell made to ring? " were the words that greeted him as the visitor, his sister Bella, entered fussily. "It rings easily enough if you pull it hard," was the curt rejoinder. "Here, give me your umbrella; I'll put it to dry in the cellar." "I wouldn't have come, only I wanted to hear from you what had happened at the hearing before the magistrate to-day." "Nothing much came out. The detective who arrested her gave evidence. A man from Tuke's also gave evidence, and so did I. It's adjourned for a week. But let's begin supper. I'm awfully hungry. I thought you'd like some wine, so I fetched up a bottle of port." "Thanks very much, replied Bella sarcastically, as she divested herself of her wet jacket. "But if it's of the same execrable quality that you gave rue last time, I'd rather make myself a cup of tea. I didn't feel well for a whole week after drinking

that last stuff." "It's the same quality, and a very good quality too," answered her brother doggedly, "Then you can keep it for your customers. I hope they will appreciate its flavour." "It's all the better for me if you don't like it, he answered with calm indifference, sitting down and beginning to carve. In manner there emi.sted .a .marked similarity between the-brother and sister, but in appearance they were quite ;epposite, . Bella was ern4 and

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

-- DEAR NELLIE When the weather is Bo uncertain that a fine Sunny day will be succeeded by one of snow and hail, it is impossible to wear anything very spring- like, but quite desirable to make a change as re- g.srds millinery, which should now be altogether °righter in tone. A crisp, dainty little toque, somewhat solid in texture, just solves the difficulty, and carries one on to the latter end of May, before which it is rarely possible to wear summer attire.

A very stylish hat has a hr.. _ ...oinposcd "tirely of pink roses—not very seasonable at this tune of year—closely massed together and a brim of folds of rose-colour gauze twisted dexterously to.und turban-fashion. A big cockade of shaded Prlnk glace silk sad two brown quills stands up ,'lgh at the left side, and the brim is raised by folds of the silk. Not quite so gay is a hat of the oarrie shape, whiefe has a crown of periwinkle-blue fancy straw almost hidden in frills of glace silk of the same shade, loops of which with the fashion- able gathered edges are also arranged at the side. lii this hat the inevitable bandeau under the brim Is of velvet blossoms of a kind completely unknown to florists. Many dressy capes are of black chiffon covering deep pink or some other colour that assimilates with the rest of the toilet, but these are all short, and, though fussy and dressy, virtues essential in Most items of dress now, they will neither be long for important looking. But it must be a woman's own fault if, wanting one, she cannot find a be. Coming outdoor garment this year. We shall all renounce them as much as possible for the dresses 'encourage going out "in one's figure," as we are all pleased to do when the weather permits. We put op a year or two to our age when in the summer time we don a mantle, and so most of us prefer to have a cape or tippet, that can be slipped on in a moment but only when absolutely necessary.

-e have for some weeks past been seeing the pretty little simple mantles and jackets which have come in as the general wear of the million, • but now the more select modes are to be met With, and very well worth seeing they are. The long circular cloak reaching to the knee in very llght fawn cloth is graceful and useful, with stitched bands of a darker shade brought up at intervals from the edge to the depth of about a quarter of a yard. It is admirably out, with a high collar, and lined throughout with cornflower-blue plod. Very dainty, too, has a small short-backed .3ecket of the same strongly woven, smooth-faced very fine cloth of the lightest stone shade, just the colour of dry sandy dust on a summer road. The sleeves are of steely-grey satin, and on this is an !l)pliquii of cloth in geometrical devices, darker ran the jacket itself, and worked with steel ceads.

A gm* and elegant walking gown in very ,dark blue serge has a tucked yoke and folded -cellar of creamy satin, and the bodice drapes over 'Slightly to the left, with soft folds of orange fieur velours just lineide. The edges of the rowers ellif3 are trimmed with plaited black silk nraid, and a d)aod of the same goes down the left of the skirt over a piping of the orange silk. is charming 'gown is finished off with a drawn lack satin hard at the waiat, and the sleeves,. Which bell 1110105,6 A the wrist, are turned up with lnge silk, and edged with the black fancy braid. th this might be worn a smart jacket in pale ar4l) Venetian cloth, which has a turn-down colla eutn, faced with white moire velours, and eiC3l4l(l with several rows of shaded silk braid othl:rh. is drab at one side, and white at the tirTll"le are some really exquisite models in 11;e8 for day and evening wear. A distinct is a blouse of maize-coloured silk, veiled cuirass of silver-grey yell lace, the design of is outlined with chenille spots of the same cate shade. The sleeves are of drawn grey ap,,ttc)llt and a cravat of maize coloured chiffon ehveare at the throat. Another lovely model is in .elenn shot silk, the prevailing tone of which is the 1:04,,te shade of sea-green, and this braided on silk b„`4lFe and halfway up the sleeves with white th 'aid, with a thread of gold tinsel running 1.4911

THE BID(-STREET IM-
ARBITRATION PROCEEDINGS,

On Saturday the arbitration proceedings in re- gard to the Feathers' Hotel were resumed at the Lion Hotel. The umpire was Mr. Wainwright, of Liverpool, and the arbitrators, Mr. Wilson, of Man- -...hester, for the Corporation • and Mr.'. C. Sutton, For the claimant. Mr. Bradbury and Mr. Sutton of Manchester, •appiared for the Corporation; and Mr. W, F. IC. Taylor, QC., was counsel for the

claimant. At the outset, before the proceedings were continued, Mr. Taylor said he wished to call the attention of the Umpire to a letter which appeared in the local papers, and which had been written by one of the leading mem- bers of the Corporation. It was really a most unprece- dented attempt to interfere with the conduct of the case and an attack on the witnesses, and considering that it was written by a gentleman who was practically a leading man in the committee which was acting for the Corporation in this case, he asked the Umpire to ex- press come opinion about the matter. It was an attack en the witness, and on the mode of conducting the case, and'written p-actically by a party to the arbitra- tion. Although he did not suppose the Umpire could do anything, vet he thought it was proper to bring the matter to his attention as an attempt to influence public opinion about the way in which this case should be , dealt with. It seemed to him to les most indecent and most impertinent. Mr. Sutton: Is not the Queen's Ben& the proper place for this P Mr. Taylor : The Queen's Bench is a long way off. The 'Umpire said it was the first tune in the whole of his experienee—and that was not a small one—that an attempt had been made by letter-- Mr.'Sutton ; May Ibe allowed to see it ? (The letter was handed to him.) Mr. Bradbury We want to get through the case. Mr. Taylor has made his protest. The umpire said it was a pity that any remarks by one side or the other should have appeared in the public press, but they would not influence him in the slightest degree. He theight he was independent enough of either aide for that matter. Mr. Sutton said it seemed to him that it was not an attempt to interfere with the case, hut was simply an attack on Alderman Sutton, that he being a member of the corporation should take part in proceedings against it. That was a very different thing indeed. Mr. Taylor: But it is really an attempt te influence our vvitneeaev. Mr. Sottun : Alderman Sutton can very well take care or himself. Mr. Thomas Tunstall,who it will be rnneinbered gave , his examination in chief on Thursday, was then cross- examined by Mr. Taylor. He said it was true that the corporation were endeavouring ,to influence the County Council to widen the bridge if they could get the power, in order to accommodate increased traffic. There was also some talk of making Warrington a County Borough. In valuing the Feathers' Hotel he had not taken Into coo sideration the water supply—he simply left out the water rate as that was all it saved in espence. Re•examined by Mr. Bradbury. He understood the water was not allowed for domestic purposes. There had not been an increase of population in the neighbour- hood of the Feathers, but a decrease, which was owing to the widening of Bridge.street, 79 or 80 houses have been removed in the process. The value of the district for business had gone worse during the last ten years, and he thought as a district for licensed property it would go worse. There was no is near ' the Feathers on which building could take Place. He did not consider that if Warrington were made into a County Borough it would increase the custom of 'the house. (Laughter.) The Lower Seven Stara in bridge. street was sold in January, 1897 for £6.250. It was at the rate of £2 101. 61 a yard. The Lion Hotel which was by far the heat hotel in Warrington was also sold in 1891 for £UOO, which with a chief rent of £75 at 30 years purchase, made £9,750, and that would make the coat per yard £3 ss. 21. This hotel had every accommoda- tion for the traffic. All the front land in Bridge-street, from Lipton's to the Roebuck had been sold at £2 10.. 11 yard, and the land behind at 101 a yard in 16E9. In reply to Mr. .1. C. Sutton, Mr. Tunstall said that he did ' Got remember the Cock, the Ship, and several other public house in Bridge-street being closed. They had not been closed during the past 25 years. With the ea- I neption of the Feathers, and ths Lion Hotel, on licensed house fronted the upper portion of Bridge-street. Mr. J. 11. Clarke, cashier at Messrs. Greereall., Whitley and Ca.'s Brewery, arpeared on subpoena, and produced 'an account showing the amount of beer sold to the leathers by that firm. 'Mr. Taylor objected to this witness, contending that the manager should have attended. The witness had no authority to disclose the hooks of the firm. 'Mr. Sutton called Mr. Stanley Wilson, assistant 'rown Clerk, who Saki that before he served the subpoena on Mr. J. H. Clarke he inquired at the brewery as to who should be served, and was told the assistant-manager. Mr. Clarke. Be (witness), afterwards called again and Served the subpeena on Mr. Clarke in Mr. Down's pres— ence, and Mr. Down said they would be prepared to produce the information required on the subrcena. eroms-examined by Mr. Taylor : It was true that the Corporation had agreed to purchase the barber's shop at Friar'-green, next Co the cottaget. He believed the price *greed on was £1,569, hut he had nothing at all to do with the negotiations. There was not only a oarber'a shop on the premises tut one part was devoted to a cycle shop, and in addition lodgers were kept at the , house. Ile did not know the area of the land. They had also bought Sutton's shop in Bridge-street for £3,000 within the last month. They gave some land in with it —the site next to Johnson's shop. The premises ennsis•ed of two shops, two dwelling-houses at the back, and a bakehouse. He could not state the area. Replying to Mr. Wilson (the arbitrator), witness said -a large confectioner's business was carried on there. By Mr. Sutton: It was an old-eatablished business, and compensation for loss and disturbance was included in the agreement. Further questions were being put to the witness about the premises, when The Umnire interposed,rernsrking that questions were being put to the witness as if ho were a surveyor or a valuer, and as he was not such evideece could net be acceptei. They were placing a burden on the shonldees of the arbitrators that was not fair, If they wanted to go into those questions they must do so in a proper man- ner. Mr. Clarke was then called, and said he had teen with Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Cr'. for 24 yasrs.fle came SS an unwilling witness. T .e amount of beer sup- plied by the company to the Feathers orss an follows In 1893 116 barrel.. in 1604 84 barrele,lB9s 68 barrels. 1896 9n barrels, 1898 (up to the preneet date) 27i her- , rels. The %aware supply for the five years from 1893 to the end of 1897 was 1 barrels of beer per week. The present tenant commenced the tecancy on the Ist of September. 1897, and from tbat date to the 22nd of Decembrr 44 barrels were supplied. This year, up to March 25th, 271 barrels had been supplied. The average for the last three months of 1897 was st barrels per week, and for the first three month!! Of WS year, ptac- ically speaking, 2 barrels 0 week.

Dr. Gornall, medical officer of health, said he had examined the claimant's cottages at Friars' Gate. Prior to that week he examined them in 1895. They were unfit for human habitation. The reason he did not take steps in regard to them in 1895 was in consequence of a consultation he had with the Towa C'erk. The scheme of the Warrington Corporation to widen Bridgc-st was brought to his notice. The houses were in such a defec- tive condition that they respired pulling down. They did not, and could not be made to comply with the bye- laws. He had also analysed the water from the pump In the yard. and in his opinion it was unfit for drinking ' purposes. He had made a report on the water which he now produced. Cross-examined by Mr. Taylor: He had been of the opinion that these iloll3Bs were unfit for human habita- tion since 1895. He was advised not to go on with the matter, that was why he did not take action. They did not get on as fast as they ought to do in dealing with this kind of property. Ho was not influenced by the Town Clerk when condemning property. The reason no action was taken in this case was owing to the fact that the property was scheduled to be purchased by the Cor- poration for street improvement. Mr. J. L. Turistall, chartered accountant, said he had examined the receipts of the Feathers' Hotel from Sep- tember 1.,t last year to January 221 d, and the total was £3OB 101. lid., an average of £l7 2s. 101. a yrreft. The tenant had not got an account of his takings after that date but a numbar of receipts had been left, and these showed that the trade was practically stationary. In Christmas week the takings were the largest, amounting to £2O 104. They were nearly tho same at the time of the municipal election. The taking had gone so low as £l5 15s.

Cross-examined by Mr. Taylor : The asserarnent of the weathers' Hotel had *Not been changed for a very long period. He had boight D thson's shop two years ago for £1,350 and it was about 319 yards in area, with about 16 feet frontage to Bridge-street._ ss s

He treated the cottages as land at £2 a yard, with £2O for the old material, making with 10 per cent. fnr eornpolnory pur- chase £283 16s. ; total valuation £2.710 164. He be- lieved a hrewar would give half is inoch mg•in for the house. The fact of the house being tied shut it out from the bent customera,and they could not get as good a price for it as if they had free competition. There were very few people who would invest in a tied house. Cross-examined 1--He had never valued any public house in Warrington before. Tie had formed his valua- tion independently of anyone else. It was sometimes the practies to take IA the gross takings sea fair rent but that depended largely upon circumstances, and he would sometimes take 1-10. He thought that the building was ill adapted for the purposes usually asso- ciated with the name of an hotel. There was nothing

in the shape of a counter. His total valuation of the premises was £2.708 The details were similar to those of Mr. runs- tall and Mr. Wilson. . _

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY,

Years ago seine Militia officers used to go there. If they did so that state of things no longer existed. They had,therefore, had as one of the main facts of the case that the house was not suitable for tha purposes of an lien, nor could it be changed without endangering the structure. they could not even convert the house into a lock-UP sham The value of the license was imme- terial,and could not be taken as a separate thing. The owner, he would point out had no means to make any alterations that might be desirable. At the Chancery trial Mr. Wilson said his fathsr did not want him to pay even £1,500, because the interest of 34 per cent, on the Mortgage would be more than the rent of the premises if let to a tenant. e,therefore, thought no reliance could be placed on the suggestion that Mr. Curran said the property was worth £B,OOO, or that another gentleman had offered £7,000 for it. With regard to the business transacted at the house,the evidence of the expert wit- nesses called for Mr. Wilson was based not upon the business as it was carried on,but upon what it ought to 1 be,and therefore there was no check on their statements. I The Corporation,on the other hand, had been enabled to furnish the court with certain data, which, though, not as perfect as they were accustomed to in cases of this kind, still was of such a character as would enable the arbitrators to form their own opinion as to what the business was. In Mr. Starkey's tenancy there was an upward movement for about a month, but afterwards the business was stationery. When he went into the house - toe found it very dlrty, and had to spend money in order to put the premises into proper condition for carrying on hu3tness. That again showed that Mr. Wilson had not the means to make any altera- tions. £l.OO was a considerable sum of money for Mr. Starkey to have spent, and he told them fraakly that he would not have spent it had he not believed that the back land would be utilised for the purpose of building , another public-house, which he would be entitled to occupy. With regard to the figures produced by Messrs. Greenall, of the amount of beer supplied to the Feathers, he submitted that if the evidence was to be relied upon the basis of the valuation made by the claimant's wit- nesses was taken away. Another fact that wts an im- portant element in the case was that Mr. Starkey was an exceptional tenant, and his wife brought with her a clientele from other hotels where she had been. In ascer- taining the average business that was done toy a public' house they must eliminate any exceptional tenant. These claims were generally put forward before experts were consulted, and that was done in this case, and the witnessea had to rack their brains to find how they could make any approach to such an extraordinary claim. They fixed the rent at £l7O or £lBO, yet the house was let to an exceptional tenant at £64 a year, It was said that a brewer might give £1.70. Then why did they not find a brewer P Mr. Taylor had the opportunity, if he had chosen to avail himself of it, of asking a repre- sentative of a brewer whether he would have been pre- pared to give any of these rents; but no one knew more than his friend Mr. Taylor when to hold his tongue. fle asked thorn to believe that the suggestion that a brewer could have been found to give £l7O or £lBO was the wildest imagination. Mr. Sutton proceeded to deal with the claim for disturbance with regard to the cab business, and asked where was the evidence that the business was destroyed 2 He submitted that the wit- nesses for the Corporation bad dealt with the matter in a very liberal way, as indeed the Corporation would wish it to be dealt with, so as to give full compensation, as the Act required, but not so that the ratepw-era should be called upon to defray extravagant and exor- bitant claims. The proceedings were then adjourned sine die. Mr. Taylor, Q.C., will speak on behalf ef the claimant at the next hearing.

div.head: ALLEGED BEGGING IMPOSTOR AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: ALLEGED BEGGING IMPOSTOR AT WARRINGTON.
A WESTON POINT MAN'S DUPLICITY.

At the Warrin-ton Police Court, before Messrs. R. Garnett and T. Birch!'ll,an elderly man whose name was given as John Morley alias S nith, hailing from Weston Point. was charged with being an idle and disorderly person and guilty of begging in Horsemarket-et. at 10 minutes to 1 in Monday afteranon. The Chief Constable said he would ask for a week's remand in order to make enquiries into prison -es ante- cedents. Ile had been going about beg.ging la a moat reprehensible manner. Ahout 12.30 on Monday after- noon Detective Barlow mad P.C. Newsy got some infor- mation which caused them to watch this man going from publichouse to publichouse and shop to shop. They followed him into a grocer's shop at the corner of Scot- land-road, and saw he had just presenl.ed a document to the shopkeeper. This document read as follows : March 28, 1898 —This is to certify the bearer to be a most worth', old gentleman. Unfortunately he has the most sad affliction of being deaf and dumb. He is the sole support of his old bed-ridden sister, when at work at his occupation, fishing net making. Of late the poor old man has been laid with the moat sorest of sickness. All who know him heti; him and it is booed and trusted other good and kmd Claristians will.—George B.(iftwiek, 4, Rose Cottage, Chapel-place, Weston Point, Runcorn. —Then follows a subscription list with the names of George Sedgwick, John Morley, Miss g. Morley,Thomas Morley, and T.W.C. for several small sums, the names being in the same writing as the appeal. The officer questioned him and he very cleverly made signs that he was deaf and dumb. On the way to the re-arion he said "Dm't expose me. I wrote the paper myself." He (the Chief Constable) flt that this was a pines of scandalous imposition and he wanted to get at defend- ant's history. Prisoner : I made no luta of it your worships. It is a pack of nonsense I scribbled down just as the young man came in.—He was remanded for 7 days.

div.head: APRIL 1, 1898.
div.p: APRIL 1, 1898.
A. WARRINGTON MINISTER'S START- LING EXPERIENCE.
CHASE AFTER A SUPPOSED BURGLAR.

Before Mr. T. Birchall and other magistrates at the Warrington Police Court on Monday, Ernest Wright, 21, Hoyle-street, a young man of respectable connections, was charged with being found on the premises of tho 11.?,v. G. Harbottle, 2, Bewsey-road, at 20 minutes to 7 en Saturday night with intent to commit a felony ; he was further charged with doing damage to the amount of 20s.—He pleaded guilty to being on the premises but denied the felonious intent. Mr. and Mrs. Harbottle were present in court.

_ The Chief Constable stated that the circumstances of this case were somewhat extraordinary. About 6.40 on Saturday evening the Rev. G. Harbottle (pastor of Beersey-road Wesleyan Chapel), was in his study, when he heard a crash of glass in another portion of his premises. He went to the scullery and found a window broken, and the prisoner standing inside. Be asked him he e was doing there, and prisoner said " I don't know." Mr.Harbottle told him he had better go away, and prisoner promptly proceeded to get through the window. When he got through he jumped over a very high wall and Mr. Harbottle pursued him into Bewsey- road, along Arthur-street, Paul-street, aryl Gladstone- street, until he was stopped by a man named Thomas Thomas, who failed to hold him. P.C. Delahay finally captured prisoner and took him to the Police Station. What prisoner wanted on the premises they could only surmise that it was for an un- lawful purpose. There was not even a servant whom he might have been sweethearting. He must have got through the ashpit into the locked yard, climbed on the windowsill and in fumbling with the fanlight have fallen through the window. The dog in the yard had been stunned. When the prisoner was brought to the Police Station he was suffering from the effects of drink but that he was not drunk was shown by the way he climbed the wall and ran. .

_ The Rev. G. Harbottle deposed that his study was at the back of his house and over the kitchen and scullery. About a quarter to seven on Saturday evening he heard a erash of glass and at first thought one of the chapel windows was broken as they had been cleaned during the day. He looked out and saw nothing. Then he went downstairs and found prisoner in the scullery and the window broken. When defendant climbed out he crossed the yard and jumped over an 8 feet wall, and witness followed "as fast as his age and infirmities would allow." He thought prisoner was under the in- fluence of drink though he appeared sober. Mr. Her- bottle finally appealed to the Bench to deal as leniently in the case as they possibly could. Prisoner was of a decent family and the punishment would fall most heavily on the father and mother. He had already been two nights in prison and had learnt a lesson which might be a lesson to him in the future. Thomas Thomas, and P.C. Delahey gave evidence, the latter stating that prisoner was shamming drunkenness on the way to the Police Station. Prisoner: I was drunk and did not know what I was doing. The Chief Constable said a great deal of influence had been brought to bear on this ease which ought not to have been. The parents bad been to first one and then another, and had also been to Mr. Harbettle, The Rev. G. Harbottle said there had been no influence brought to bear upon him. He certainly saw prisoner's father, who only offered to pay the damage. The Bench retired to consider their decision and en their return, the chairman said that he was sorry to see prisoner in this position especially from what he knew of his family. The magistrates had taken a very lenient view of the case after what Mr. Harbottle had said on his behalf, and they had come to the conclusion not to send him to gaol, but fine him 20s and costs, or a month for the offence, and order him to pay £1 damage. They hoped it would be a serious warning to him.

div.head: NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: NOTES AND NEWS.

The situation in the Far East is sow clear. Russia has obtained everything that she wanted. The diplomacy of Great Britain, and the resolution of the British Par- liament,bave been a beating of the air. Chineee troops have left Port Arthur, Russian troops have entered, the Russian flag flies over the forts, Russian forts are to be constructed at Talienwan. That is, Mancburiahas virtu- ally become part of the Russian Empire, and the parti tion of China has begun. On the other hand, the British fleet is to be mobilised in Bong Kong—for what purpose nobody knows. Nobody knows the policy of England. Nobody knows the attitude of Japan, N3body knows anything, except that Russia is a country which first determines up As a policy and then executes it.

A loss which has cost every member of the Gladstone family an additional pang ef pain during the last sad days is that of little Petz, the black Pomeranian who for nine years past has been the eonstant and faithful com- panion of Mr. Gladstone in all his walks and drives about Ilawarden. Last week, a few days before Mr. Gladstone's return home, Petz began to naive food, and became listless and depressed. On the day of Mr. Glad- stone's return he was taken home to the Castle, but it k was too late, and Petz died a day or two ago. It is a latter-day theory that " hearts don't break " with grief, but surely the case of little Petz dying because the be- loved master had left him for so very long shows that a faithful dog, at ail events, can die of a broken heart.

Mrs. Parnell, the mother of Charles Stewart Parnell' died on Saturday under peculiarly paieful circum- stances. She was sitting close to the drawing room fire at Avondale, the Parnell country house, when her dress caught fire, and she w as fatally burned before assistance could be rendered. The deceased lady was an enthusiastic Nationalist, with an outspokenness of speech which was not always to the advantage of her party, although its sincerity was never questioned. Dur- ing most of her later years she lived in America, but she came back to Ireland to die in the old home.

In connection with the subject of oysters and sewage Sir William Priestley relates a recent very unpleasant experience of a lady residing at Bowdon. Going to buy some oysters, she asked the shopkeeper if they came from healthy surroundings, and was candidly informed 1 that this could not be guaranteed. " Why." it was added," they smell so bad of sewage sometimes that we cannot keep them in the shop, but they get clean if you put them into a little salt water far a while." Sir Wil- liam points out. however, that it needs more than "a wnile "to purify oysters that have lain in sewage. charged water. Give them, however, ten to fourteen days in pure sea water, and they will clean themselves absolutely even from germs of typhoid. According to this excellent authority, there is n. o danger of typhoid from eating oysters which have lam under the influence of more sewage. The danger arises when such sewage contains active germs produced by some typhoid case.

The " Standard" says :—We believe that the view which is now generally taken by naval autherities, and which found acceptance at the recent Conference on the subject, is that in case of war between this country and any European Power merchant vessela will have to depend more on ':heir own exertions for their safety than used to he the case in past times. The aid method of convoying is out of date under present conditions, and the most that can be asked from the State is • system of " patrolling" by swift cruiers such as might be or- ganised between this country and ths Cape, if , the Mediterranean—as might easily be the case in time of war—became practically closed to British commerce. Speaking eenerallv, straits mid shallow wateis will have to be avoided, and British merchant vessels will have to keep as much as possible to " blue waters," and trust to their own speed for satevy.

(the" Dilly News "re- The Spanish people can still marks) find plenty of money for their amusements, and particularly for the amusement of bull-fighting. The three most famous bull slayers at the present tihle are Mazz tntini, Reverte, sad Guerrita. The first took part last year in 68 fights, killing 163 bulls ; the second in 71 lint, killing 180 bulls; and the third in 78 fights,killing 147 hulls. ktizzantini's earnings for the year wr,re 396,000 pesetas (£15,840), those of Reverte 276.000 pesetas (£11.040), and those of Guerrita 256,000 pesetas (£10,240).

Another success has been scored by a portion of the &win-Egyptian force in the Soudan. Gunboats carrying the 16. h B ittalion arrived at Shendy on the 26th inst ond captured the dervish reserve depot there, burning' the plaze and destroying the forts. No casualties occurred on the attacking Rido,but the dervishes lost 160 killed and IRS prisoners, besides animals, ammunition, cattle. and grain. The present military situation is described by Reuter's special eorrespondeht at Ras iludi camp as unique. The dervish force is practically beseiged in its entrenched position M the dense bush at Et Hilgi,and is starving. The Khalifs has ordered Alah- mnd either to attack or return to Orndurman,and he has replied that he cannot do the former for want of food.

ThP anld of Alaska. on which the attention of man- kind is just now fixed with brilliant anticipation, may net, in the and, turn out to he the ereatest treasure which that land possesses. The Alaskan forests appear to be among the most valuable in existence. They are of enormous extent, partly in Alaska and partly in British Columbia, and are probably the greatest continu— ous body of timber of the cone-bearing or pine family in the weed, almost unmarked as yet by the axe.

Prnfessor Snelbelhel says the quality of " nerveless- ness" distinguishes the Chinaman frem the European. The Chinaman can write all day, work all day,. stand in one position all day, weave, heat gold, carve ivory, do infinitely tedious jobs for ever and ever,and discover no more weariness and irritati an than if he were a machine. This quality appears in early life. There are no restless noughty boys In China. They are all appallingly good and will plodd away in school without recesses or re- creation of any kind. The Chinaman can do without exercise. Sport or play seems to him so much waste labour. He can sleep anywhere, and in any position—. amid rattling machinery, deafening uproar, squalling children' and quarrelling adults.

div.head: PROTEST BY COUNCILLOR HENRY ROBERTS.
div.p: PROTEST BY COUNCILLOR HENRY ROBERTS.

On Friday at the Warrington Police Court before the Mayor, Councillor H. Ibberts, and Councillor J. Smeth- urst, Mr. Shine )ck applied for a license to sell intoxi- cants at the forthcoming exhibition in Parr Ball, for 12 days. Be asked for a lilense from Monday, March 28 to April 2, and from Aptil 4 to April 7, and then for the llth and 12th.
Councillor Roberts : I object strongly. Do I under- stand this is for the Trades Exhibition ?
Councillor Shit!cock : Yes.

Councillor Roberts: I have not the slightest objoc- I tion to you having any license for any special occasion because I know you will conduct it satisfactorily. I ob- ject on principle to this exhibition being associated with anything of the kind. I don't like the Parr Hall being continuously and persistently associated with matters of this kind. As a member of the Parr Hall Committee I tbject, and if I had known that Mr. Hooper was going to I apply I should have had something to say about the whole matter then. I understood Mr. Hooper was corn- ng to do something which would have special reference o the trades of Warrington. The thing is not carried non philanthropic lines, and Mr. Hooper wants a pro. t, but there is no necessity for a special license. Councillor Shillcock : Mr. Hooper has nothing to do with this. I take it on my own responsibility. Councillor Roberts: I quite understand that and I have confidence in you, but I don't think the sale of drink is necessary in the public interest. . _ _ . . .

Councillor Smethurst : I endorse Councillor Roberts' opinion so far as that goes. The Mayor : We wish to meet you in a reasonable way, and I can respect the opinions expressed by Coun- cillor Roberts. We will grant you from 5 o'clock p.m. until 10 p.m.

div.head: STARRT FATAL/TT AT WARRINGTON._
div.p: STARRT FATAL/TT AT WARRINGTON._

An inquest was held at the Parade-room, tram- street, Warrington, on Tuesday, touching the death of John Taylor, aged 6, of 62, Turner-street, who was run over by a cab on Monday, and died at the Infirmary.—Elizabeth Taylor,wife of Robert Taylor, 62, Turner-st.,said that the boy received his injuries about 12.15 on Monday. He was coming home from school down Ash ton-st. A neighbour told her that the boy had been run over, and as she got to the door she found the boy walking on the footpath. He was taken to the Infirmary, When he came into the house all he said was " A master's run over me." The driver of the cab, when he came for the boy, seemed sober.—William Potts, 5, Tilley-st., said he saw the accident as he was walking along Haydock- street, and saw the boy run across the corner of Ashton-street. He ran against the horse, fell, and the front wheel went over him. Witness picked him up. The cab was coming down Haydock-et, and the boy ran out of Ashton-st. The driver pulled up as quick as ever he could. Witness did not think any man could have pi Iled up quicker.—Percy Wood, driver for Messrs. Maginn, corroborated the previous witn.ss. The boy ran straight out, of Ash- - ton-street, and into the horse. Witness pulled up in two yards,and after taking his fare to the station- . returned and conveyed the boy to the Infirmary.— Eliza Cowley, nurse at the Infirmary, said deceased was admitted at 12 30, and died at 430.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental Death."

IN. his speech at Rochdale Lord Spencer Wednesday, Lord SPENCER d at Rochdale. with the political questions of t day in a commonsense fashion. His way looking at things is, we believe,thst of nine out every ten well-informed Englishmen. There war

eVidently quite willing to accept the honour of a lest on the Beard of Guardians it they were not op- Defied but they would not face a contest at any IWO. In one case there were three nominations for one seat, but each of the candidates on finding that other Richmonds were in the field hastily Withdrew so that the township is left without any gtlardian at all. There has been nothing of that Sort in Warrington. Each of the wards has either get its representative or will have the opportunity of selecting one on the 4th of April. Toe most in- teresting of the three contests will be that in Fairfield Ward between Dr. McCarthy and Mr. Pilling. A meeting will be hel rn euPport of Dr. McCarthy on Wednesday uext,but We do not hear that jr. Pilling intends to address any public gathering. That is rather singular. Mr. Pithug claims credit for his six years' service on - the Board of Guardians yet he refrains from giving an account of his work to his constituents. It can- not be said that there is nothing particular to speak about. There is the important question of public- house assessments, with wnich Mr. Pilling is very 'Closely concerned, as the lace Chairman oi toe As- Beesment Committee. An explanation of the des - Parity between the assessments of the " tied" houses belonging to brewers and those owned by the Corporation from an ex-chairman of cite Assess- Merit UorunntLeo Would be of gleiLL tuLerest to rate- Payers who knew that they Ultra:sell es, at al vents, are fully assessed. v, There wasa visible evidence of the unity of the raugelical Free Churches in Warrington on Sun- 'ay When the annual interchange of pulpits took Place) followed later on in the evening by an United , `4rataineion Service in Bewsey-roan Wesleyan Church. In the" Wycliffe Church Record " for this toonth, the Rev. J. Yonge makes the following corn- bent on the movement;—" This annual custom is deserving of cordial approval and sympathy. ately. There appear to be a number of people, especially in London, who have come to the ex- traordinary conclusion that it is about time this country began to fight with somebody some- where. There is some confusion as to the other party in this international duel. Sometimes Germany is pointed to as the enemy, then it is France, and at other times it is Russia. But, as Lord SPENCER points out, and as most sane people thoroughly realise, a war between power- ful 'rt. io The he o last t: ht nations nations is no light matter. Wars in the past have been horribly distractive; the next war between bably excel almost evarythin; known in history of human lea din, stthqeuawrotrelrd of ial l cporno- tury has been on the whole a time of peace, but ' for all that many of the ablest and most ingenious, minds of Nuropo and America have been engaged in perfecting weapons of warfare which will be placed in the hands of soldiers and sailors in the. next war. These weapons will be used with. deadly precision if the armies of Europe are again arrayed against each other on the battle field. Lord SPENCER therefore does well to cen— sure the talk of war which is almost criminal in its recklessness. Dior° is one e xcuse to be made for these Jingoes of ours. They have met with some rather bitter disappointments lately. They have asked the Government, which they look upon as practically their own creation, to perform impossibilities in the field of foreign affairs, and some members of the Government have more than half promised to oblige them. Disappoint- ment was, therefore inevitable under thesis cir- cumstances. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER and one or two other Cabinet Ministers have, for instance, hinted that they would rather go to war than allow Russia to do certain things in China,but now that Russia has appropriated both Port Arthur and the ever-famous Ta-Lien-Wan they find that they are not in a position to carry out the sanguinary threats of a month or two ago. As a matter of fact thc real grievance to be laid at the door of our government is that it has sub- jected this country to diplomatic humiliation, or , the appearance of diplomatic humilation, in a per- fectly unnecessary way. T his comes of not know- ing its own mind. Germany and Russia have both had definite objects in view and in carrying out theirplans they have gone straight to the point. But the British Government appears to have been caught unawares, and its actions have been of that vacillating character which Mr. JOHN MORLEY condemned in his speech last week. The two topics of domestic interest to which Lord SrEercnn referred were those of education and Home Rule.ln connection with the former subject he declarcdstrongly in favour of popular control 1, of all state-aided schools. He is dead against taxation in aid of voluntary schools without repre- sentation on school committees,and his p*aounce-- ment is one more indication that a change of Government will mean a change of policy in regard to national education. Lord SPENCER may also be regarded as throughly " sound " on Home Rule. He sees clearly enough that al- though this question has, almost of necessity, fallen into the background for the time being, all the conditions which make Home Rule of one kind or another inevitable still remain unimpaired. He does not believe that the local government which the present Government proposes to bestow on Ireland will supersede the Irish demand for the control of national affairs ;on the contrary he thinks it will only give additional force to that demand.

Soma interesting particulars The Great City. with respect to London were given in a paper read before the Auctioneers' Institute on Tuesday. The great metropolis can claim a very respectable antiquity. It is said to have been founded 1,107 years before the birth of Christ, 350 years before the building of Rome, and 600 years before the fall of the Assyrian monarchy. At the present time the district under the control of the London County Council contains a population of five millions and includes 600,000 hOuses. London is a capital city in every respect. I is the largest manufactuiing town in the Empire the greatest port, the chief literary and scientific centre, as well as the chief commercial, banking, shipping, and insurance emporium of the world. Its suburbs contain a larger population than the whole of Ireland. If London were deserted to- morrow it would require the whole of the in- habitants of Seotlani and Wales to refill it. So populous and busy are the central parts of the city during business hours that the problem of locomotion is one which urgently demands a solution. The traffic now daily entering the city is upwards of three quarters of a million persons, and it is ex- pected that in a few years it will be a million and a half. How to find a means of ingress and ogress for these increasing crowds of people is the question which confronts the municipal authorities and the schemes that seem to find the greatest favour are an elaborate system of subways and the development of an electric tram system.

RUNCORN CYCLING CLUB. Tha members of the above club opened their season on Wednesday evening by a " social" held at the Wilson's Hotel. Mr. Booth occupied the chair. A pleasant even- ing was spent, songs, tel., being gives by Messrs. F. Mack, G. Whinyates, Neild. J. Charlesworth, W. Shaw, Oultram, and Booth. Mr. Chrimes proved an efficient accompanist. ST. PAUL'S MEN'S BIBLE CLASS. At the weekly meeting of the above class held on Sunday afternoon, Mr. R. H. Posnett delivered a very instructive address on "The Bible," to a large gathering of members. Mr. Ben Crosby gave a solo and a selection on the organ. A number of new membere were en- rolled.

BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL Gtrum.3 The weekly meeting of the above guild was held on Wednesday evening, the Rev. J. Osborne in the chair, a paper was read on the subject " Dickens in Poetry (Hood) " by Mr. W. Millington. The speakers were Messrs. Speakman and Beck and Miss Clayden. A vote of thanks was accorded to the essayist for his paper, on the motion of Miss Cameron, seconded by Mrs. H. Handley. CONFIRMATION SERVICE AT RUNCORN. Dr. Jayne, Bishop of Chester, held a confirmation at Runc3rn Parish Church on Friday evening, when 154 candidates wore presented, viz, 98 females and 56 males. These were drawn from the parish of Runcorn (including the Parish Church,St. Michael's, Mersey Mis- sion,and Weston), and the parishes of Holy Trinity, Hil- ton, and Aston. RUNCORN BETHESDA P.S A. The monthly open meeting of the above seciety was held in the B thesda Chapel on Sunday afternoon, Mr. James Handley, C.C"Presiding. The speaker for the day was Mr. Wood, from the Crescent P.S.A.,Liverpool,who gave an interesting address in support of such institu- tions as the one that had brought together such a splen- did audience. Mrs.Timperly sang the solo "Where shall we spend eternity ?" and Mr. T. K light gave a cornet solo. The choir also sang "As the hart pants."

div.head: POLICE CASES.
div.p: POLICE CASES.

At the Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday morning, Robert Jones, a sailor,was flied 20i for being drunk and disorderly in High-street on the 2301 March. P.C.Bow- yer proved the cases.—Eizebeth Darker was committed for a month for being drunk and disorderly in D evan. shire-square, on Monday night, and also for using obscene language in Paol-lane on Saturday night. This was prisoner's 47Qh appearance before the Court. STOCKHANI ANNUAL PARISH MEETING. The annual parish meeting was held on Tuesday night at Mr. Clarke's house, Stockhana. Mr. J. Clarks was re- elected ceairman for the ensuing year, and Messrs. J. Clarke and R. Nickson were re-elected overseers. Tbe Stockham charity for the year 1897 showed the receipts to be £9 19s, and the expenses £5, given to widows,left a balance in hand of £4 19s. Mr, A. Woodier (the clerk) W3S instructed to write to Mr. C. L. Evans thanking him , for his support to the charity. ST. EDWARD'S RUNCORN. At the abeve church on Sunday the Rey. Father Stanley of St. Mary's, Latchford, was the priest in charge for the day. At the evening service he alluded to the distress prevalent in Ireland and appealed very strongly to his hearers for support of the no inr funds which had been started in different parts of the country. The Rev. Father Gore, pastor of St. E lwarde, also took Father Stanley's place at Latohford, en Sunday. BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. On Wednesday the last meeting of the Brunswick Mutual Improvement Society took place under the pre- sidency of Mr. Sinister. The room had been taetefelly I decorated by Mr. Jones of High-street. Tea had been provided by Mr. Nancollis, after which there was a short entertainment. Slags were given by Messrs. A. Cooke and A. Holding, Messrs. Bisbrown, Johnson, and Rev. J. A. B. Malvern, and a humorous sketch by Mr. W. Jones. Messrs. J. D. Jones, D. Fowlds and Saunders testified to the benefits received through the medium of the society. Games of various character were afterwards resorted to under the efficient management of Messrs. W. Jones, and J. Millington. Tbo proceedings were thoroughly enjoyed and the meeting was a splendid success.

div.head: BRUNSWICK BAND OF HOPE.
div.p: BRUNSWICK BAND OF HOPE.

The last meeting of the session in connection with the above society WV3 hold on Tuesday evening, in the Brunswick school. The mile items on the programme was a lantern entertainment illustrating the story en- titled "Two golden lilies." The views were very good and quite pleased the young people. Mr. J. U. Pickthall manipulated the lantern. A double quartette party' which included the Misies Williamson, Leathwood Macdonald, and Hailing, and Messrs. Withingtor, Saunders, Johnson, and Bisbrown rendered Jude's com- position, "At evening ere the sun was set," and whilst each verse WM being sung they were illustrated by the lantern. "The Village Blacksmith," also illustrated on the screen, was sung in style by Mr. G. Johnson, and two recitations were admirably glean by the little Miss E. Johnson and Master J. Parry. While they recited, their photographs were thrown on the screen. Speeches were afterwards delivered by Mr. James Etiggin, an old poineer of the temperance movement in Runcorn, and Mr. J. D. Bisbrown, the conductor. During the session over 50 pledges had been taken.

- RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. At the Runcorn Petty Sessi,ios on Monday, before Messrs. A. R. N)rman and W. Timmins, Reece Hughes and Peter Brown, of Runcorn, were charged with com- mitting a breach of the peace by fighting in Bridge-st„ Itancorn, on the 19th Mart:b.—P.C. Ellis proved the case, and defendants were each bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay the costs.—Enoch Shaw, a bay, residing in Surrey- rez.was charged with throwing stones In Greenway-road, to the damage of passengers thereon, on the 18th March.—P.C. Gregory gave evidence, stating that he cautioned the defendant at 4-30 and at five o'clock he again found him throwing spoues.—Defendant said other boys were throwing at him.—P.C. Gregory said Ithat was not so.—Defendant was fined ss. and costs.— John Cook:, teamsman, of Frodsham, was charged with driving a horse and lurry in the Chester-road, Sutton, on the 23rd March, without a lighted lamp attached to the vehicle.—Sergeant Richardson proved the case, and defendant was fined Sc. including costs. William eousins,of Runcorn, was fined ss. for neglecting te send his child regularly to school. ST. Joules PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH, RUNCORN. On Wednesday evening a festival of congregational music was held under the conductorship of Mr. W. A. Edwards, conductoi of the Liverpool Festival. The meeting was a very successful one, the hearty and in- telligent manner in which the various hymns were taken up by the whole congregation giving evidence of careful training. This church has already a good reputation for congregational singing, and the conductor spoke highly of their efforts on this occasion, and no doubt this fes- tival will have the effect of still further improving it. The conductor also highly complimented the choir for the very efficient manner in which they had acquitted themselves, particularly in the quick intelligent response given to his interpretation of the various items rendered. Mr. J. E. Warburton, the choir master, had had charge of the rehearsals. Mr.Elwards is an excellent conductor and well worthy of the position he holds as conductor of the Festival of combined churches in Liverpool. The organist Mr. James Richardson, presided at the organ, and by the able manner in which he discharged the onerous duties contributed in no small degree to the success of the Festival. The pastor, Rev.T.Sidney Morris presided, and addresses were also delivered by Rev. 0. D. Jones of Liverpool and Mr. E. J. Hughes of Birken- head. The singing of the Doxology brought a very en- joyable meeting to a close. A RUNCORN BOATMAN SUFFOCATED IN HIS FLAT. On Monday, Mr. Sampson, city coroner, held an in- quest touching the death of Charles Spencer, 43 years of age, master of the flat Primrose,belouging to Mr. George Hooton, Brunswick-street, Liverpool and who lived in Gilbert-street, Runcorn. It appeared from the evidence that deceased was a healthy man. On Monday of last week his flat was lying in the Waterloo Dock, and when he and his wife went to bed in the cabin shertly after nine o'clock there was a fire burning, one ventilator and small scuttle being oven. Early next morning he awoke his wife, asked her the time,and Raid he must get up for a drink. As soon as he got out of bed be exclaimed, "Lord help me," and fell to the floor, the wife at the same time becoming unconscious. When she came round she found her husband being removed from the abin by a police-officer, who had been called by a flat master named Plumb, who had noticed that deceased had not made lain appearance at the usual time on the deck of his flat. Plumb said that he perceived a smell of sulphur in the cabin, but this was not unusual in a cabin where a stave had been burning. Spencer was removed to the Northern Hospital, where be died on Wednesday last. Ds. Coates, who had made a post-mortem examination of the body, stated that in his opinion death was due to suffocation through the breathing of some foul air, the exact nature of which he could not ascertain. I verdict to this effect was returned by the jury.

CHARGE AGAINST "DARLINGTON," A RUNCORN
RUGBY FOEtWARD.-HEkVY FINE.

- - - - Before Messrs. Charles Reynolds and A.Thomas at the Fredsham Petty Sessions, en Wednesday, Frederick Darlington of Frodsham, and a forward of the Runcorn Football team, was summoned by his wife Annie, for assault. Mr. Churton, solicitor, Chester,appeared for the com- plainant. Be said the defendant was a labourer at the Western Point Chemical Works. The assault complained of was as brutal as it possibly could have been. The parties had been married eight years and there were four children. For two years of the married life the defend- ant bad been a teetotaler. He had an attack of influ- enza and some one told him to take bottled stout. Since then, when in drink, he treated his wife very badly. The defendant was a member of the Rancorn Football Club, and frequently came borne drunk after the matches. 0 1 the 26% February be treated his wife shamefully, and he asked their worships to grant a separation order to Cite complainant. Annie Darlington said defendant was a labourer earn- ing 30.5. a week. When they were married he was a tee- totaler, and for six years they lived at her mother's house. M ceased to be a teetotaler about two years after marriage, and almost every Saturday he got drunk and came horns and abused her. He was a member of the Runcorn football team. 01 the date named he was not drunk, but he had had some drink. He came home in the afternoon and his tea was ready for him. Witnese was sitting in his chair when he said " Come out of that, you have not long to live." fle then struck her in the face deld knocked her to the ground. She had the baby in her arms at the time. Defendant kicked her in the face and also in the side. Her face was black next morning, she left the house the same night, and had never lived with him since. She had been attended to by De. Selby. Defendant had been in the habit of abus- ing her before. By the defendant : She could swear that he kicked her. She did not know what he did it for. He had frequently cline home drunk. Martha Forster, mother of the cemplainent, said she was sent for on the date named by the defendant's mother to come to his house. She went down and saw a pool of blood in the helve. Wttnees then went for the sergeant. Mr. Churten then real a letter he had received from Dr. Selby whicn stated that the complainant suffered from lose of blood, abrasions below Deo left breast, in- juries to the rib etralc, and %leo from greet pain. Witness continuing, said defendant had abused com- plainant very frequently in her preeence. Since assaule was committed she and her four children had beou liv- ing with witnese. By the defendant : She had seen him etrike her be- fore. She saw him throttle the complainant ou Jubilee night. Sergeant Clays depesed to being called to the house on the night in cpeation. The complainant was lyireg on the sofa. Her face was very much disfigured and swollen. The table was covered from top to bottom with blood. She was also spitting blood. Ho did not see the defendant there. This concluded the complainant's case, and the d. fee- dant then gave his version of the affair. Be said he was generally away from Frodshain on a Satarday. Oa the day in qiestion, he stayed at home. He had been met in the street by certain people and they had given him bills. These things he always left to his wite to attend to. When he accused her of not having paid them, she denied that she owed any. She aggravated hi n until he struck her. He did not kick her, nor did she fall on the floor. Oa the morning following the as- sault, he went to her mother's house and apologised to his wife for what he had done the previous night, and asked her to come home again. His wages were 28s. a week and he gave his wife as., and he bought his own clothes. He admitted the assault,but he was very sorry. He saw his wife in bed on the 27th February after the bother, and she promised to return home with him at night. When he went for her at nieht she was up, bat things had (elite ch impel. His me:her-in-law- must have heel "her say "iii the matter, and complainant re- fused to come home. He had a good home for her to come to and he assured the Bench the thing would never occur again. The Chairman said defendant had no earthly right to treat his wife in the manner he had done, no in later whether she wester: his naoney or not. They had decide I to fine him £2 end 11. e. 61. costs, or one m eatlfe im- prisonment with hard labour in default. Mr. Charton before the close of the Court applied for a reparation order. Mrs.Darlingto i said the defendant got 30 a week she wanted to have the eustody of the four children. She asked for 14ei for her own and tha children's mainten- ance.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF UUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF UUARDIANS.

- • - The fortnightly and last meeting of the old Board was held on Tuesday afternoon, at the Workhouse, Dutton, Mr. J. Knowles presiding. There were also present Mr. A. R. Norman, J.P., the Rev. Dr. Gesteldi, with the members of the Rural District Council, and Mr. J. Ash- ton (clerk), and Mr. G. F. Ashton (deputy clerk). THE ASSOCIATION OF POOR LAW UNIONS. Mr. H. E. Lawrence, secretary to the Provisional Com- mittee of the Association of Poor Law Unions,forwarded a memorandum and copy of the bill which had been in- troduced in the present sesoicrs of Parliament, to provide for the establishment of a Poor Law Union Association for England and Wales and to enable Boards of Guar- dians to contribute to the expenses of such association. The object of such association is to take action in all matters affecting the common interests of poor law Guardians througheut the country, to promote and as- sist legislation in which they may be interested, and to fulfil on behalf of Boards of Guardians similar functions to those performed by the associations of municipal Corporations of County Councils, and of District Coun- cils on behalf of the bodies which they represent. The minutes were approved of and itwas also decided to request the local parliamentary representatives to support the Bill. ARMY PENSIONS. On the invitation of St. George's Miesion, London, the Parliamentary Committee decided to petition government so to arrange army pensions that these may be paid weekly and not quarterly, it being pointed out that the meney was frequently at once spent in drink and for tne rest of the quarter the man were des- titute. The recommendation was adopted. THE BOARD AND HABITUAL DRUNKARDS. The Parliamentary Committee had considered a letter from the British Medical Association with respect, to habitual drunkards. The association advocated (1) power to substitute curative and reformation treatment of criminal inebriate offenders for their existing ineff,m- tive imprisonment in jail; (2) power to seclude non- criminal habitual drunkards, with due regard to the liberty of the subject in special curative institutions; (3) curative seclusion, at the public charge, for poor habi- tual drunkarks; (4) appearance of an inebriate desirous of admission to, and detention in a Retreat, before one justice or other authority, instead of nefore two justices as at present. The Parliamentary Committee recom- mended the Board to pass a resolution urging the Government to bring in their promised Bill for Amended legislation for Inebriates. The recommendation was agreed to on the motion of Mr. Mclntyre seconded by Mr. Norman. THE CONTRACTS.

The following tenders i;;;;Ci-PTil-iing the House with goods, AO, were accepted :—Coffins,John Barrow ; coal, Evans arid Co., Elaydock ; funerals,Booth and Son,Run- corn : cartiog, W. Grounds ; coke, Frodsham Gas Com- pany; boct and sniies. Jooeph Ilizley,Runcorn; clothing, Fletcher and Lee,Warrington ' • milk,Fred Weir. Walton ; butchers meat, Singleton and Stephenson, Warrington ; drugs, J. H. Weston,Runcorn ; grocers,W. Collier, Run- corn.—Mr. Norman suggested that in some branches of the tenders matters would be somewhat simplified if the chief items were more particularly mentioned than the small ones. For instance in grocery and drapery there was no need for little items which meant practically nothing to be put in. On the other hand the big and important items were the chief things and guided them in the matter. Taking grocery, bread was the chief thing,and mustard was a very little item. It would save much time if the Master wocld take the principal items, and the small items such as mustard and vinegar could be taken for granted.—Mr. Mclntyre : They can by that reduce the prices on the big articles and then make them up on the small ones.—Mr. Norman : It is a diffi- cult matter. I have been Oleg through some of the contracts and it takes a great deal of time in unwrap• ping the samples. If they knew what the main things In the house were they would soon be able to judge.— The matter then dropped, it being understood that it would be brought up at a future meeting of the Muse Committee. •

div.head: GAS STOYE EXHIBITION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: GAS STOYE EXHIBITION AT RUNCORN.

In the Bethesda Lactate Hall, Runcorn, on Mond y evening, there was opened an exhibition of the well known Wilson patented gas cooking and heating stoves, gas fires,gas washing coppers,gas laundry irons,lx.:. The first day's proeeedings were opened on Monday by Mr. Samuel Taylor, J.P. There was only a poor attendance, probably owing to other attractions in the town. Mr. Taylor said he had very great pleasure in intro- ducing to them Mrs. Pitcher, who would give them a practical lecture in cooking. He thought he kaew isetter than to say anyttaieg about cooking before so in any ladies. (Laughter) If he attempted he wls sure he would be out of lois boundary. But,if he did not know how to cook be :certainly could tell when a thing was well and properly cooked. Ha might say that his people had had some experience of cooking with a gas stove at his house, and he could assure them that they would not part with it on any condition. I: was looked upon as one of the most useful pieces of furni- ture t ley had. It saved a great deal of labour and was perfectly clean as compared with what the old ranee used to be. As they knew open fires were not at all agreeable in summer time, and gas stoves, he believed, were only just being found out to be of great service and benefit to the householder. They had now got them so perfect that in going around the room that night and seeing the various stoves he was surprised to sem the great perfeetion to which they had now got them, and , he firmly believed that before many years passed there , would not be a single house without a stove. 83 con- venient were they, that they need not light up until their j ,ints were ready to be put in. Therm were over 600 penny in the slot meters in use in Runclrn to-day, and be learned that Messrs. Wilson bad stoves which were most suitable for the cottage and small houle- holders, and could ba had on very easy terms. He was certain that in summer time it would be a great advan- tage to those householders who could do with %ut the open fire for som-thing lace six months in the year. When the working people of Runcorn and other towns get to know of the benefits that are ta be derived from gas stoves, h wis certain that they would be vary ex- tensively used. He was certain that Mrs. Pitcher would give some valuable information on cookery, and he h‘d very great pleasure in introducing her to them. (p- -' plause.) Mrs. C. F. Pltcher, who is a first class diploing s and principal of the Streatham Scour! of Cookery. London, was attired as a cook and was surrounded with al the nelossary articles f m cooking, then gave a pract'cal lesson on the following :—lnexpensive cakes, supper dishes, and SAV mries. The exhibition was opened eve 7 morning, except M mthy, and closes to-night (Friday). On each afternoons and eveoing lectures were delivered by Mrs. Pitcher. 'no prom iters of the exhibitions in order to put the stoves to a practical test allowed per- sons to use them free of charge for baking bread, pastry and joints. The room was arrayed with a plentirul supply of stoves of various designs. Toe " Wilson " patent stoves have been grant-d 40 awards including eleven gold medals. The cooking strives can be had at the Runcorn Gas Office at rash prices from 245. to £9 49., and fixed free of charge.
