INTERESTING GATHERING.

The annual seci tl gathering iii c inneeti en %tech ee, Paul's Wesleyan Choir, Runcorn, was held .n Wedne-- day ii lot, at Mr. Riley's Cite, Bri Ice-street. 'retire was a large attendance of nynnbers including a few friends. A su nptums meet eras placed before the guests he Mr. Riley and his ;taff,who proved themeelvoe to be etficieet caterers. T tking, advantage of the oppor- tunity, the members of the choir after verde made a nresentation to Mr. Bun Crosby, who is shortly to take 1 up his residence in Garston, he having got an appoint m-nt there as headmaster of the new W-sleean schools. In th • ab4ence of Councillor G. 11 Krkhan Mr J. Birkett took the chair. He was supp e-ted by the R. J. Clifton, kr. F. J. Norm R Merri.c,and Mr. T. T. Burrows. Mr. Birkett said it cave him very great pleasure to be chairman of that meeting, the objet of which was to present to Mr. Greeley the gifte that appeared on the table. He had known Mr. Crosby fora very long time, and his connection with the chair w .8 a very long and honourable one. He knew that he (Mr Crosby) woul took back with priie on the deya he hid spent with St. Paul's choir, which he theught no choir coul I come up to in efficiency. Mr. Morris said he had a very pleasing duty to tier- form—that was to present to Mr. Crosby on behalf ef the choir, a silver mounted baton, and on behalf of several members of the congregation a in no= dress ine Case with silver mounted fittings, and four sp'on- deity bound music b 'eke' He said it hid been a pleasure to work with Mr. Crosby during the time he had been conductor, and he was very Beery that he was leaving chem. However, he wished him and his fnnly every succese. (Loud applause.) The Rev. R. J. Clifton said as a minister he had been delighted to work with Mr. Crosby as eonductor of the choir. His geniality and the energy displayed by him both in the choir and as a laymen was of a very high class indeed. Mr. Norman Said he had known the recipient of the presents that night from a boy, and knew him to be heart and soul in the work of St. Pull's choir. Every- his • he did was done well, and they ceull rely on hi n c PI .e a thing which required tact and delicecy. Ar. Burrows also added he testimony to the work performed by Mr. Croabv. On rising to respond, Mr. Cresbv was loudly cheere 1. He said he was very deeply touched by such eepree- sions of good-will as had been uttered that nig'it. Hie connection started with the choir about 25 years age as a bey when he sang alto, and lie had his opinion now that the choir was the best in the north of England. No matter what he had to do outside the choir business he made it Die duty to be present every Sunday morning at chance at twenty minutes past ten, and alsn at the practice on Thursday evenings shortly after eight. The work he had performed had not been a duty hut a labour of love during the whole time he had been connected with them. (Loud applause.) The company then joined in singing " For he's a jolly good fellow." Games, ke, were afterwards indulged in until the small hours of the following morning. The presents were four beautifully bound copies of music of the following works : " Mount of Olives," Ros- eines " Stebat Mater," " Last Judgment," "The Golden Legend," all Dhvello's edition. The inscription on each of the volumes is :—" Presented to Mr. B. Crosby by a few of the members of the St. Paul's Wesleyan congre- gation,on the occasion of his leaving the town, as a slight recognition of very valuable services rendered in conoection with the choir. Runcorn, March 30:11,1898." The inscription on the baton was Presented to Mr. B. Croehy by the members of St. Paul's choir. div.head: LOCAL LAW CASE.
div.p: LOCAL LAW CASE.

RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL, AND THE LONDON AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY. An appeal by the defendants in this action from an order of Mr. Justice Stirling, dated the 28-h of January last, was opened on Wednesday, before the Master of the Rolls and Lerds Justices Rigby and Vaughan Wit- Mr. Buckley, Q C., and Mr. Hewitt appeared in support of the appeal, and Mr. Crippst Q C., and Mr Shearman for the railway campany. The hearing of the one was adjourned. The hearing of %he Me was proceeded with on Thurs- day. Their lordships gave judgment without calling upon courtsel, f.tr the rasp.eident. The Master of the Rolle held that the judgment appealed front was right. That judgment declared that the land drains, ditches, and sewers of the plaintiffs were not vested in the defen- dants, and restrained them from connecting their sewers with those drains: Tres defendants had no right to turn their sewage, into the drains of the plain. tiffs unless those drains were sewers vested in the defendants under the Public Health Act. That the drains were sewers within the definition of the clause seemed tolerably plain, and the Public Health Act said that all existing and future sewers within the defendants' district should vest in them, and be under their control. But there were exceptions, and amongst them were sewers made and usod for the purpose of draining, preserving, or improving land, ueder any local or private Act of Parliament, or for the purpost. of irri- gating land, arid in his opinion the drains in question came within the first part of that provision.—The Lords Justices coecurred.—The appeal was dismissed with costs, but the operation of the order was suspended for three months.—The Master of the Rolls suggested that the district council should Come to an understanding with the railway company.

RUGBY FOOTBALL.

There is little food tor comment this week—at any rate from the doings of the Warrington Club—thouzh there is the surprising event af a win which the Wil- derspudlians managed to accomplish against Manning- ham. Victory has been more and more rare of late,but apart from this the SaCC‘293 was the more palatable as the visitors obtain° supremacy the previous Saturday on their own ground. Too much credit cannot be taken f..r this success, however, as the Warrington men had only 14 men to conquer, and about ten times as many spectators to cheer them on.

Altogether there were some peculiar features about Saturday's match. To begin with there seemed a good Probability that there would be no match at all, as 4-30 arrived without a sign of the visitors on the field. An hour's wearyohiverir.g,waiting on the Causeway thinned the crowd out rapidly so that it was not surprising to had the smallest "gate" of the season assembled when tne match did commence at 4-35. The "Tykes" on arriving at Manchester found themselves in a position to say "We dunno where we are" for their train had de- parted without them. This necessitated their squatting on their haunches and soliloquising; on the buffetings of fate till the next train Warrington-wards put in an ap- pearance. Possibly it may have occurred to them that it was an idiotic idra to go on to Warrington at that un- earthly hour with only 14 men. The laws of the Northern Union however are not to be trilid with, and the be- lated Valley Paraders completed their programme. They showed a praiseworny diligence too, and arrived at the "Norton" in various stages of undress, About five minutes saw them trooping to the ground with a display of enthusiasm which to say the least, was not marked.

The remaining feature of the match deserves a situa- tion of "splendid isolation " in this column equal to its uniqueness in the records of the club for the present season. Warrington actually won by the unprecedented margin of three g 3 ;19 to nil. Why ! for over 3 months place kicks and all other sort of kicks have been so un- productive that the spectators, and players even, havt scarcely troubled to see to oval to its destination, so easily foreseen was it. Theu all at once the team goas mad—metaphorically—arid rubs in a trio of first-class goals. No wonder pthple rubbed their eyes, marvelled, and whispered that they had thougtht the days of miracles over.

The day was exoesilingly cold and windy, so no one expresse I surprise at the alanniugharn team turn- ing out in WhitP, summer like costumes, instead of their customary warm coloured jerseys. By the way, what an infliction it i 3 to hays to write two such beastly long names as Manningliam and Warring,ton every few minutes. Clubs ought to be prohibited from carrying such weighty titles. I say weighty, because I saw the visitors' general factotum lugging savagely at a gossa- mer like football bag with the huge club name on it. He seemed much over work.A. The two words might ad- vantageously be clipped down to their first syllables— Man,'!War,"—with striking appropriateness. Con- tractions in print are unfortunately funiddeo, se I must necessarily "grin and lmar". the strain after voicing my protest.

Bolt tetma had a V..ry bak &vision, so there was nothi:ig to m dro comparisons with there. Isherwood and FI tilam atHentees from the selected Warrington fifteen,Co,sq and It tdcliffe being drafted in. The opening stages of the game were confined to the Winningham half, as the wind blew very persistently, and strongly that way. Mr. Referee Underwood,who is not worshipped down here, appeared to have a desire to propitiate the critics by 'awarding a number ot free kicks to Warrington. The first was right in front of the posts, and Duckworth landed a goal with a nonchalance which suggnsted that he did that sort, of thing daily, and twice on Sundays. Then followed a lot of falling down, knocking on, and general scrambling on the line, all to no purpsse, until the next opportunity for a gc al came. Mason took the pie-co and with a terrific "do or die " kick, recorded another goal for Warrington. Another spell of " bits o' aw soorts " and then the ball came sail- ing in Cross's direction. This player showe.d that the epidsinic was spreading by lowering the goal far the third time, with a clover drop-kick. The second half of the game calls for little comment. There was no scoring, and though the visitors had the advantage. they mehi such a poor Use of it that thoy never looked like saving the game.

All through, the m Itch was a or exhibition of foot- ball, and I don't know that I ever saw Warrington play with more lack of cnrthination. Duckworth was ex- ceedingly erratic in taking the ball and passing. while even " Smack " B ,te seemed off form. R adcliffo and Cross bath shaped well, and H mow moderately. Mason and Naylor were the pick of the forwards, the farmer especially having hard lines iu his attempts to score. Hepburn, Gaunt, b,nd Wilkinson were prominent in the visitors' team. Their passing was superiot to that of Warrington, far from exe€ hence an it was, Tt,e for- wards did well considering their weakness in numbers.

Oldham's chances of bringing off the " double event " were knocked on the head at Batley on Saturday, when the clever combination from C4ttonopolis tot by a try to nil. Batley's splendid forward pity brought about Oldham's downfall. Batley rushed the scrummages all through the second half, and but for the splendid de- fencv of Arthur Lees and Lawton, Oldham would have lost by more than one try. Few expected Bratnley to have a chance at Salford, and the R ,cla won easily by 4 tries to a goal. Bradford it was thought would beat Broughton Rangers. This they did,though not until they had endured a period of suspensl, br the Ringers after being five points behind got on leval terms, and had the wind with them. Finally a wonderful goal by Cooper agaiwit the wind gave tiaNn a passag3 into the penulti- mate round.

The semi-finals in the Northern Ueion Challenge Cup, on 4pril 9th, proini.ie to be Particularly interesting. Batley will have a hard nut to crack in Salford. and Bradford will find Widnes an awkward tern to defeat.

After being out of the cup competition since the first round it was hoped that Warrington might perchance get one of the semi-fl lois, but they have again gone astray. I suppose it is thought that Warrington is not the cnntre of a big Atlll zh population, but all the same there would be a file crowd from the neighbouring towns if Warrington aid been selected. The enclosure could be made to li 'I b.tter ground could not be found. Warrington's claims are too obviously slighted in many respects by the N.C. Committee.

At a meeting of the committee of the Northers Union in Manchester on Monday. the most important business was the fixing of the venues for the Cup semi-finals on Saturday, April 19. Toe arrangements made were as follows :—Salford v Batley, at Oldham : Referee, P. Ferrer (Elalifax) ; touch judges, J. Underwood (Wigan) J.B ruckshaw(Stockport). Br adferd v Widnes at Halifax: Ff. Referee, W. la`Cutcheen (Oldham) ; touch judges, IL Hutchinson (Wakefield Triuity), and H. Waller ; (Brighouse Rangers). 'The final, if played n.tween two Yorkstire ulUbs, will talcs place at kleadingly, Leeds otherwise on the Broughton Ringers' ground.

To-day the League matches are re.umed and War- rington journey to Broughtoo. The tarn i 4 these as was Lhoson laiit week, and should give the Ringers a good game, as the latter are by no m-ans brilliant in back play. Why Duckworth is kept in the centre is a bit of a mystery. He would be far more usqul in the wing next to Hallam, and possesses a fair amount of speed. Centre is plaint! not his place- Bite might do worse than try this alteration. 4111,-
THE DEATH OF A CHILD AT HAYDOCK.
THE PARENTS SUMMONED FOR NEGLECT. FATHER SENT TO PRISON.

A case in which considerable interest was mani- fested was heard at the Newton Petty Sessional Court on Thursday when Thomas Henry Marsh and Jane Marsh,of 36,Vista-lane, Haydock,were cearged at the instance of the National Society for the pre- vention of Cruelty to Coildren with having between the Ist. ebruary and the 11th March wilfully ex- posed their newly-born child in a manner likely to cause it unnecessary suffering and injury to health. The magistrates on the Bench were Mr. T.J. Gilles- pie (chairman), Colonel Wood, Captain Withington, and Mr. Brown. The defendants pleaded not I guilty.—Mr. J. W. Knowles prosecuted on behalf of the society and said the defendants were parents of an infant child born on the Ist February and which died on the morning of the 11th March. A coroner's inquest was held two or three days afterwards. Although he didn't think he was justified in using words which the Coroner made use of, yet he thought he might go so far as to say that the proceedings were the outcome of the Coroner's words. What he intended to prove was that this child was healthy at birth but it had been very much neglected and its surroundings had been bad. The principal evidence the magistrates would have to rely upon would be that of Dr. Hay ward's. His evidence seemed to bring the defendants almost on the verge of manslaughter. The doctor said that from the post-mortem examination he had made of the child be was led to the conclusion that it had been occasioned unnecessary suffering and had not been properly fed. He also told the Coroner that the neglect had contributed to the death of the child, but he could not positively say whether it was the actual cau,,e of death or not. If the doe- t had been in a position to say that it actually caused death, the defendants would have been brought up on a charge of manslaughter. The police were in a position to say that the male defendant took a great interest in tootball and took very little or no interest in his home. He frequently went home about eleven o'clock at night and sometimes later. He was a lazy man who seldom worked, and the case was as near the point of manslaughter as one possibly could be. Martha Prior a neighbour of the defendant's was the first witness called. She deposed to visiting the house when the child was born and finding very little fire. On a second visit she found the child crying very bitterly, and eventually advised its re- moval to the doctor. She looked after the family for ten days. At its birth it was a bonny child,. weighing she should think, from seven to eight lbs. There were no Beres on the child when it was I born. _ _

Mary Ellen Reardon, 47, Vis a-lane, stated that she went into the house after the child was dead and washed it. It was in a very dirty condition and lay on a bed that wasn't fit for a dog to lie on. She had frequ.natly given the children of the defendants food, and described the man Marsh as of a lazy disposition and one who (14 wed hie family to suffer by his laziness. Elizabeth Stirrup deposed that she saw the child on the morning of birth, and also 10 days afterwards. It vras a healthy child at birth, and even when it was ten days old. Neither of the defendants she thought at- toradA to their children its a proper manner. The man was a laz7 fellow and didn't %yolk as he ought to do,and his wife was rather inattentive to the nouse and the children. Had it not been for the generosity of neigh- bours it was her opinion that the other two children would net have been alive now.

Dr. Hayward, of ylock, stated that duriee his at) Bence on the let F bruary the child was sent to his sur- gery and attended to by his assis ant. The reason of the child being sent was that they were afraid of it hav- ing convulsions. He did not see it until March 12th when by the order of the Ceroner lie made a post-mortem examination. As far as the outer part of the body was concerned he found it in a very emaciated condition. On weighing it he found it to be 51 be. in weight. The average weight of a male child at birth was not less than six or seven lbs. and at the age of five weeks the average weight ought to he from nine to ten lbe. The state of the :kin showed that the child had been in a state of filthy, reelect. 'eternally the stomach an l intestines were absolutely and entirely empty, and but for some slight signs of inflammation of the left lung he must have come to the conclusion that the child died Item the neglect. As it was lie could not say that the child actually died from neglect hut there was no doubt that the neglect had greatly to do with its death. —ln answer to questions by the male defendant, the doctor said unfortunately he had attended him for influ- enza. Sernetimes wh he had called the defendant had been unweleend on occasions he had given him certifi- cates to get money from the colliery. P.C. Teomesen spoke as to the character of the male defendant, and described him as a" hanger-on "at a public house, and the football field. He had seen the de"end int coming home at 2 o'clock in the morning.— P.C. Rewcliffe said the man was a lazy fellow, and sel- dom worked. The male defendant then addressed the Court in his own defence. Be said he could have proved by the hooks of the Colliery that he had worked as hard as any ,man. For 30 years he had worked as a collier, and it was only last winter that he stopped work,when be was attacked with Mann and rendered unfit for work. He did not know that he was going to have the charge of lezMeee brought against him or he would have got evi- dence to prove to the contrary. TII9 Chairman said the defendant had had plenty of time to get whitever evidence he required. The defendant said he only received the summons on Monday: The Chairman remarked tilt a day was sufficient for the defenden^ to get information to prove his case. The defendant was then sworn, and said that last summer with the exception of a week he followed his work regularly. It was only within the last few years that he had been attacked with illness. There was plenty or :food meet ed to the ileum and he had earned money in various ways. He was unable to go down the pit owing to fainting bouts, and he had had to be carried to the pit's mouth on several occasions in conse- quence of them.Ele had worked for the football club and money had frequently been given to his boy Sydney by Mr. Platt, the landlord of the Waggon and Horses, and the money was taken home to his wife. The defendant nrocedded et some length to describe his exertions at home. Frequently he had gone in,taken off his jacket, washed the children, scrubbed the floors, and done any job he could in the house, especially when his wife had been confined. He did everything he could for his wife and children. If the beeks of the cellery were examined it would be found that he could show as good a result as many men could.—Mr. Knowles produced bills from the celliery showing that the detendant bad not earned as much as others, and that he might have earned more if he had exerted himself. In cross-examination, Mr. Knowles brought out the fact that a subscription amongst colliers had been raised for the bent of the defendant. Theenoney the defendant said had been spent in food for the children. The female defendant corroborated her husband's statement. Two of the children were also called, and they spoke to their father having been very goad to them. They had never seen him drunk. • I three children—Elizabeth (11), Eward ne'grlheectdeedfetnhdeiarnts were further charged with having (7), and Walter (4). Mr. Knowles again prosecuted in this case.—lnspector McAteer gave evidence as to visit- ing the holm end finding the children in a dirty and neglected condition. There APS very little furniture in the house and it was in a filthy state. After evidence had been given by P.C.'s Greety and Rawcliffe and Mrs. Rearden, the magistrates retired to consider their decision. On returning. the Chairman said the magistrates had given the case full consideration. They were unanimous that it was one of the most painful and disgraceful cases which had been brought before them. For neglect of the child,the male defendant would have to go to prison for three months with hard labour,and for neglect of the other children, one month. Al retarded the wife, the magistrates believed that she acted under her husband's influence, and she would be discharged.

PILFERING FROX A PENNY-IN-THR-SLOT METER. On Friday morning at the Warrington Police Court, William Henry Leather (18), was charged with stealing frcm the lock-up shop of Hugh Flinn, Grove-street, be- tween the 23rd and 24th March,the sum of 12s. 81.—Fle pleaded guilty.—A further charge was preferred against him of stealing from Robert Leather, 68, Wiawick-read, 4s. 4d. —To this charge he pleaded not guilty.—The Chief Constable said that in the first instance defendant was charged with shop breaking,but the charge was reduced to stealing. Prisoner lived with his father at Grove-st. They occupied a tenement which was part and parcel of the shop occupied by Mr. Hugh Flinn. There was a door outside wh,ch communicated between the prisoner's house and Mr. Flinn's shop but /ilia was always kept locked on the shop side. About 9 p.m. on Wednesday Mr. Flinn's assistant locked up the shop sad put 235. in a box on a shelf behind some other boxes. In the money were a half-sovereign and a half crown. The following morning he found the box hod been broken into and these two coins were missing. The door commu- nicating between the hou3e and shop also ehowed signs of baring been broken open, and information was given to the police. Suspicion fell upon the prisoner and be was arrested. Enquiries were mode, and it was found that he had been spending money rather freely. When charged he said " I wish to make a clean breast of this affair. I got up about 5-30 and came down into the kitchen and pulled the dresser away from the door leading into the shop. I then unscrewed the catch the lock fits in. I went into the shop and got the box which contained the cosh,where I have seen the man put it, through the wisdow. I got 12s 81 and put the box back and secured the door. I afterwards went to Earlestown and spent the money with some pals." With reference to the second charge, the I Chief Constable went on to state that be bslieved prisoner pleaded not guilty became he disputed the I amount and net the theft. Between Christmas and the middle of February prisoner was lodging with his uncle at 68, Winwick-road. In this house was an automatic gas meter. About the middle of February it was found that the meter had been opened and instead of ccntain- ing 33. or 4s. it only contained id. Prisoner's uncle spoke to him about it and asked for a certain key. Prisoner handed his uncle the key, and it was found to open the I meter. The youth admitted tampering with the meter, I and when chargen admitted taking I.e. 6i. in copper from the meter.—Robert Leather, 69, Wlnwirk-read, corroborated. Be said his thnught there was no key that would open the meter. His wife made a communication to him which caned him to open the meter. Instead of 4s. Of Be. he found only Id. He had since had to pay 4e. 41 to the Corporation.—The Mayor (to prisoner who had borne a defiant atti-ude all through) : What have you to say ?—Prisoner : Nott ing.—The magistrates sent him to gaol for a month's hard labour in each case. Wmotassus THEFTS FROX • WARRINGTON CLOTHIER. On Monday morning at the Warrington Police Court, before Mr. T. Birchall (chairman), Councillor J. Shaw Green, Councillor Smethurst, and Mr. S. Wright, Joseph Lingley was char red with stealing from the shop of Charles Paikin, 39, Difersey-st., between January 28 and March 23, seven suits of men's clothes, five pairs of trousers, a man's overcoat, two silk hand.. kerchiefs, and a shirt, value in all about £l6 --Prismer pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable said prisoner was originally charged with shop breaking, but that charge had been reduced to larceny in order that he might be dealt with that mornlng. Prisoner had been banging about prosecutor's premises for the last few montbs,do- log odd jibs, and Mr. Paikin at lapt told him that he would not want him. Prisoner still continued to harg about the premises, On the night of the 22ad prosecutor's premises were broken into by the kitchrn window being forced from behind, and a number of articles ef clothing were stolen. The followlvg night about eleven o'clock Detectives Barlow and Rop wen in the neighbourhood making observations when they heard the breaking of glass at the back of Mr. Paikin's prernises,which are surrounded by a wall sfl Sin high. One of the offieers managed to look over Mr. Paikin g gate and saw the prisoner and 4 man named Pridden, standing on a box tampering with the window. The officer climbed over the e‘te and caught both prisoners and brought them to the Police Station. Toe shirt and muffler were found OR Lingley,and in one of his pockets was the silk pocket handkerchilf. A number of env .1- ones with Mr. Paikin's name prin, eI on were found on Pridden. Priiden's hand was bleeding, and there was some blood on the window. Ungley was in possession of eleven pawntickets, which related to a nurnb.r ot pledges of new suits of clothes. Altogether 13 pledg ‘y had been recovered by the police and each had been Peag'm identified as stolen from Mr. Paikina'ses' T police bad had considerable trouble,had s therm i en carried out systematic robberies. Eight diff.rent had been got to pledge the art'cles. Mr. Paikin wont 1 tell the magistrates that £1.6 would not represent any. thing like the worth of the articles he had missed during the past few menthe. Linelay hod made a profit of about £5 85.—Lingley. and Frederick Pridden,43 Lord Nelson-at, were now charged together with being on the enclosed premises of Charley Paikin with intent to commit a felony on March 23rd.— Pridden pleaded not guilts'.—The Chief Constable said he had recited the facts of this case in the last case.— Detective Barlow proved the case against Priddei, who stated to the magistrates that he thought the other man lodged there and he had merely given him a "hIZ-uP" over the wall. Lingley was committed to gaol for four months, and Pridden for two months.—The Chairman complimented Detectives Barlow and Roper en the I Till with which they had managed the affair.—Two of the pawnbrokers, with whom the goods had been pledged entoseqaently appeared before the magistrates,and asked if the money they had advanced would be returned to them.—The Chief Constable said their Worshipo hod power to make an order to that effect.—Mr. S. Wright expressed an opinion that as Mr. Paikin had allowed Lingley to loiter about his premises ho ought to be the sufferer,if any. The other magiqrates concurred„and it was decided that the goods should remain in the vols.'s- by Mr. Paikin. sion of the pawnbrokers until redr.orn.,l

They had been In harness for thirteen hours.—Miss Litton said she saw the horses in Moore. They were v.-ry tired, and the paid for them be be put up for the night as the driver had no money.--Inspector Greatrix said that on Monday morning, from information received on the 14th March.he went to Mr. Nelsons, Windsor- road, Liverpool, the owner of the horses. He examined the horses then, and found the brown gelding was very weak and in poor condition. It was by no m-an. in a fit state to work. He examined the second one. which was a grey mare. It was in poor condition, and had an old wound On the off side of the shaulder, which was very painful, end the officer drew the attention of Mr. Nelson to it. After some words had passed between them, the defendant struck the complainant over the left eye. The blow was so severe that the complainant was stunned and she fell against the door. div.head: WARRINGTON v. SIANININGIIAM.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. SIANININGIIAM.
A RESULT REVERSED.

The return match between Warrington and Man- ningham, was played at VVilderspool on Saturday in rough weather. It will be remembered that the same two teams met the previous Saturday on the Valley Parade Ground, when the homesters were victorious by 8 points to two. Warrington had a big share of the attack even then and it was thought that they should have no difficulty in avenging themselves at Warrington. This they succeeded in doing by a majority of 6 points to nil, after a very scrambling game. The Manningham team put in an appearance an hour late, having missed their proper connection at Manchester. When the game stared at 435 there were only about 1,000 specta- tors present,a record small gate, for the season. Mr. 'Underwood, of Wigan, had charge of the whistle. and the players lined out as follows, neither side being full y represented and the visitors were a man short.
Warrington J. 13051(!OW,_ full back; Moores,Cross,
.. , . . . uckworth and Radcliffe, threequarters; J. T. Bate, and R. Bate, half backs ; Naylor, Deakin, Taylor, Mason, Morrison, Hill, Fairhurst, and Hatton for- wards. _
- Nlanningham: Fawcett, full back Popplewell, flebden, Hepburn, and Thomas, three-quarters Gaun;. and Wilkinson, half backs; Proctor, Bradley, Ward, Newall, Clarkson, Johnson and Clegg, for- wards.

Warrington won ths toss and Proctor started for Manningham against a strong wind. Boscow'a return landed the ball well in Manningham'a half,where several scrimmages took place. Efsbden made a clever mark off a punt by Cross, but the gale prevented him gaining any ground. Manningham were soon forced back on their lines and Bate getting away from a scrimmage handed to Naylor who got to the line but failed to get over. A stiff struggle under the posts was ended by Gaunt kicking strongly to the quarter line. Radcliffe secured the oval in the loose and had a drop at goal but his kick was charg, d down. Mason snapped the bail up later and made a strong dash for the line but was well tackled. Play again waged under the posts and Gaunt for a little over-anxiety to keep Bate out was penalised and Duckworth landed an easy goal. Strong play on the part of the alanningham forwards transferred play to centre, but they were soon sent back by a strong dash and punt on the part of Morrison will looked like scoring. Wilkinson foolishly punted and Boacow made his mark, the kick being entrusted to Mason who landed a fine goal amid the cheers and shouts of surprise of the home spectators. Another penalty against the unfortunate 114anninghamites was taken by Morrison, but he failed to raise the ball. A spell of loose play ended in Mason kicking into the nsxt field when he had a fair chance of scoring. Then a brief spell of defensive play was force] on Warrington, Wil- kinson making an unsuccessful bid for the line. The hams lot soon returned to the other end, and here Duckworth missed the ball with a clear course in front of him. Mason tried again at a penalt,- but failed,liep- burn marking splendidly. Fawcett saved pluckily in front of a strong dash. Cross received from a punt, and coolly increased Warrington's score by a really fine drop kick. Tne score at half time was 3 goals to nil in favour of Warrington—.a remarkable score for them considering their goal kicking abilities. The second half was uninteresting as far as foot- ball went, though there was much to smile. Taylor started and some weak kicking by the visitors led to an invasion of their territory. Gaunt tried a penalty I kick but nothing came of it, and Warrington pressed again. Mason was prominent with several dashing runs but was tackled promptly. Fiwcett kicked badly in touch, and Warrington's kick out looked like piercing the Manningham defence. Again Mason snapped up the oval and dashed clean through his opponents and over ' the line,only to be recalled for some informality. A pas- sing movenient ended in Radcliffe getting over, but I again there was something amiss with the effert. Play fluetuated considerably to the close, but the homestess more than held Ur. ir own, and won by 3 goals (6 points) to nil.

RUNCORN V. ST. HELENS. This engagement was played off at S. Helens on Saturday before 300 spectators. The frost prevented Runcorn playing at St. Helens on Christmas Day, and the boisterous weather on Saturday rendered good foot- ball out of the question. Runcorn only had three of their regular forwards playing, whilst St. Helens had Siddall, of the disbanded Recs. team, in their threequarter St. Helens had the advantage of a strong cross wind. After a little give-and-take play Traynor intercepted a pass, and ran half the length of the field to the Runcort( line, where Runcorn half tackled him, but could not prevent him crossing the line. To everybody's sarprise the referee disallowed what seemed the clearest possible try. The Runcorn nacks now got going, and some clever passing now endangered the Saints' lines, but Foulkes and Traynor defended well, and Houghton being co'- lared with the ball in his own 25, Runcorn were put in a tight corner. The ball came out to O'Hara who dropped at goal, but it failed [a rise, and Taylor Sashed through the ruck of the Runcorn team and scored.Tray- nor added a goal. Some lively play followed the restart, and if the Runcorn wing men bad made the most of their opportunities the score would have been equaltzsd, but Warder and West both failed at critical moments. Houghton was defending finely, and I gained ground for his side repeatedly. A combined at- tack by Traynor and Doherty carried play to the Run- nern quarters,and the ball was bobbing about in a pro- miscuous fashion when Siddall slipped in and scored a pretty try behind the posts. No goal followed,and ends being then changed it was felt that the eight points lead was none too safe against the wind ; but the tactics of the home team were changed, the ball being kept close and the forwards left with the hulk of the work. Run- corn often took up a strong attacking position, but were never really daneerous,whilst St. Helens missed several goed openings through over eagerness. Th• dribbling of the home forwards was generally well backed up,and Traynor on one occasion cleverly piloted the ball past Hc ughton, picked up in front of the posts, and despite the Runcorn full back's close attentions scored a good try. The game continued to be keenly contested, but somewhat uninteresting, and finally St. Helens were hailed winners by one goal three tries to nothing. Rovconv A v.VVltsvorr.—at Ranenrn. B )th teams turned up short, and S•voral had to he found as substi- tutes. Lightfoot kicked off for Weston against the wind Moston returning, Wilson dribbled the ball down to Riley.who saved by kicking into touch. Lightfoot broke away for Weston, but he WAS tackled by Nickson. Weston pressed. W, flayter,who was playing full hack, being tackled with the hall in his possession. Fish and Sutton got SWAT, for Weston, the latter being tsckled on the line hr Gayter. Half time : Runcorn 4 nil, Weston nil. Langley feyseed for Runcorn,Lightfoot returning Weston pressed Gavter saving. Sutton scored for Wes' ton,no goal resulting. Final : Weston one try (3 points) Runcorn A nil.

WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB v. RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.

The return game between these two clubs was played on the tables of the latter on Saturday evening, and resulted in a wia for the visitors by 218 points on 12 games. The Warrington team arrived at Runcorn about four o'clock and were hospitably entertained by their opponents, Mr. Barnes, the steward, providing an enjoyable tea. In the games which followed the visitors had much the best of it, as the fact that Runciorn only won 3 out of the 12 clearly shows. They appeared to be, as one of them aptly remarked "in a state of blue pink," and were unable to obtain the revenge for the defeat at Warrington which they had fondly anticipated. Before leaving for the 11 25 train Mr. E. J. Mitchell, steward of the Warrington Liberal Club, expressed the pleasure which the matches had afforded and thanked the Runcornians for their hospitality. div.head: CONOERNINU FEEBLE FOLK.
div.p: CONOERNINU FEEBLE FOLK.

WE all knew thdit—the feeble folk ; those who are and are understood to be, in poer health. Exactly what ails them nobody knows, or pretends to know ; and when the local doctor is inquired of, he either shakes his head or says, " Sort of general debility," and leaves the impression on your mind that he could go deeper into the case were it not for certain professional reasons Yet most of the feeble folk do not bother much with doctors. They know what to do for themselves quite as well, or better, than the medical men do, and so invest the money the doctor might otherwise get in flannels and occasional short purneys in very mild weather. And thus they go on living and doing light tasks, when they feel like it,for year after year—never in sound health,yet reaching old age without ever having a single attack of serious illness. Strong and vigorous men and women— vastly better insurance "risks," as one would suppose— are stricken down in the neighbourhood, and the feeble folk attend the funerals until Darwin's doctrine seem reversed, and we have an example of the survival of the unfittest. Bilious persons, and women with periodi- cal attacks of sick headache, or heart trouble,are of this kind. Generally, they are small eaters, careful abeut their diet and sleep, and blessed will a valuable set of cAnservative habits. They are apt also te appreciate the Importance of keeping the feet warm and the bowels open. Hence their immunity from those acute diseases which prostrate the naturally strong—who neglect early symptoms, and, ignorant or over-confident, become vic- tims of some malady that is quickly fatal, or the source of chronic suffering, before they realise that they are in the slightest danger.

The latter is the process by which so many who start out in life with constitutions good for flfty or sixty years of work and enjoyment,brealc down in mid-career, or sooner with seetninzly hopeless dyspepsia and the various orzanic ailments and disturbances that are part i‘nd parcel of it.

Permit me to.tlay to aid another to the nUmerou illutitratinns of this which have been cited in these little health discussions of ours. " For many years," writes a !sly, "I sal suffered from general debility and indigestion. I had a languid, drowsy, sinking feeling at times, as if I had no strength or energy left in me. MY appetite was poor, and after meals I had pain and weight at the chest. Whatever nourishment a took gave me no strength, and I felt al- most too wetk to get &limit. Now better and now worse, I continued like this for years. I rfreOvlrl no benefit from any of the remedial I employed until I made use of Wither Seigel's Curative Syrup. This medicine seemed to put new life into me. I could eat well and my food no onger distressed roe. By taking an occasional dose of it I have since kept in good health.l have recommended Mother Seigel's Syrup to many of my friends, who have benefited by its use. You can publish this statement as you wish, and refer anyone ta me. (Signed) (Mrs.) Martha Anne Eustace,4o, Dvidingtnn Grove, Kenning- ton Park Road, London, August 4th, 1897."

" Having always a weak digestion," says another, " I have obtained much beneit from the use of Mother seigel's Sornn. I hava used it in *he family, and for friend's, for twelve years. I have much pleasure in recommending it whenever I can. You are at liberty to publish this statement if you think it may be useful. (sicfnern jemima K. Br )ml.v, wif.4 of Mr. B. Bromley house decorator, 275, High Streot,Brondesbury, London, August 1Crh,1897.'

No doubt the feeble folk of whom I have spoken suffer commonly from a, mild form of indigestion, modi- fied in its effect by their habitual rantion. The other class, who have brought on them lel yes severe and body- wrecking dysnepiia (often cornolica,ed with liver, lung, and kidney troubles) by darios,, tho enemv in the fear- lessness of previous health and strength, are still mere to be pitied. A meeting of the above was held in Bewsey-street Chambers on Wednesday afternoon, Mr. W. Houghton, J.P., presiding. There were also present Messrs. J. Dignum, J. Ball, J. Warburton, T. Halton, T. Mather, J. W. Knowles. Mr. J. C. Sutton (deputy clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), Mr. W. Owen (survevor),Mr. F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector).

MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT. Dr. Sephton, medical officer, presented his annual re- port, which stated that the area of the district was 15,549 acres. It bad been reduced by the extension of the municipal boundary of Warrington, so as to include Little Sankey with a population of 2620. The estimated population to the middle of 1897 was 10,397. the num- ber of deaths reported was 149, and births 284, against 148 deaths last year and 278 births. TUB gave a birth rate equal to 27.3 and a death rate of 14.3 per thousand of the population. The infantile death rate was slightly higher than last year and equalled 147 8 to a thousand births. Twenty deaths were caused by the seven prin- cipal zymotle diseases, which was a little above the average. The zymotio death rate was equal to 1.9 per thousand. There were no cases of smallpox in the dis- trict during the year.—The report, which included that of the Inspectmr, was passed.
BURTONWOOD AND ITS REPRESENTATION ON THE GUARDIANS AND DISTRICT COUNCIL

The DEPUTE CLERK said there was a suggestion from the parish of Burtonwood about the increase of their re- presentation on the Rural District Council and the Board of Guardians. The subject was really a matter for the County Council. The Clerk had written to tho Clerk of the Burtonwood Parish Council advising them that the course they shou!d pursue was to apply to the County Council to divide Burtonwood into two wards, and it now rested with them to take that course if they desired or lot the matter stand. The CHAIRMAN : It was on'y incidentally a'luded to at the last meeting. Mr. Wannuarots said there was a meeting of the Bur- tonwood Parish Council the previous night and they agreed to let the matter stand. ThP CHAIRMAN said he thought this would be best un- less they could get the pariah oivided into two wards.

--- In the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, War- rington, on Thursday last week, the annual general meeting of the governors of the above mentioned institution was held. Owing to the unavoidable absence of the President through illness, Mr. F. Monks, J.P., C.C., was voted to the chair. There were also present : Revs. Canon Willis, G. B. Thurs- ton (rector of Lymm ),11. V. Pigot, E. C. E. Carleton, B. Percival, W. H. Drummond, Doctors Langdale. (house surgeon), Bowden, Richmond, White, Mrs. Willis, Mrs. Litton, Mrs. Pickmere, Mrs. F. W. Monks, Messrs. John Fairclough, J.P., John White J.P., Vere B. Davies, George Thompson, J. D. Buck- ton, James Emmett (representing Cheshire Lines Committee), Joseph Taylor, John Roberts, Mr. J. L. Tunstall (hon. secretary), and Mr.°. Leigh (assis- tant secretary).

. LETTERS.. The Hon. SECRETARY read a letter from Mrs,J,C,Parr,. in which she stated that Mr. Parr was in bed with influenza, and begged her to write saying how much be regretted not being able to preside at the meeting. Be wished to express his regret to the acting Chairman and to the meeting for his absence. Be had read the annual report with much satisfaction. He also enclosed a letter he had received from the Rev. Father Wilson.—The letter ref,rred to was then read, in which the writer stated that he found there was a vacancy en the Hoard of Management,' and offered himself as e Candidate for the office.—A letter was also read from the Rev; John Tonga, stating that he was soray nn engagement at Manchester prevented his attendance. It appeared to him a matter much to be regretted that the Parr Hall Committee had let the hall for an attraction on Sunday last, on the OCCISion of Hospital Sunday. From what he heard there was a considerable falling off in the collections taken,manv people having gone to the Parr Hall. Would the Parr Han Committee make up the deficiency? - - --

THE ANNUAL REPORTS. The following report of the Board of Management was presented :—" The hope was expressed in the last re port of the Board that arrangements would be made which would enable the contributions of the Working men's Committee in future to be received within the financial year SO that the income taken into account might correspond with the actual receipts of each year, ono the forestalling of future income might thus be avoided. The Board regret to have to say that this has been found impracticable,and they have therefore come to the conclusion to credit the contributions of the com- mittee in the accounts of the year during which they are paid over to the institution. It will therefore be found that although the very handsome sum of £824 103. 91 has been received from the Workingmen's Com- mittee since the close of the year, no contribution by them is included in the accounts for 1897, and the debit balance of the expenditure and Income account has con- sequently largely increased. The income for the past year, leaving out of account the above-named sum, was £1,518, and the expenditure £2,328 Os. id. The donations received amounted to £7l 63. 11d, only, against £605 183. in the preceding year. The expendi- ture shows an increase £233 13s. 9d.; the chief items of the ems§ being drugs, dressings, &c., £146 03.1 d.; food, £29 18s. 3d.; repairs ancrirenewals,27o 6s. 3d. The aver- age number of beds occupied during the past year was 34 1-5, compared with 32 in 1896 and 28i in 1895. The cost per occupied bed was £54 103., against £5l 183.31 in 1896, and £5B 17s. Bd.in 1895. The Board have to re- cord with regret the death of the late Mr. T. Starkey Smith, M.B.i F.R.C.S., one of, the honorary consulting medical 'officers, and of the late Mr: Thomas Morris, Fa.s., a member'of the Board of Management. Whilst the contributions by the Workingmen's Committee show handsome increases year by year, the greatest possible difficulty is found in keeping up the general subscription list, and the Board earnestly appeal to the public to assist them in this matter. It may be interesting to note that the list of subscriptions has only increased during the last 45 years from al3 to £332, whilst the work- ingmen's contributions have risen from £l3B in 1877 to £824 10s. 9d.in 1898. Dated 11th March, 1898. SENIOR HOUSE SURGEON'S REPORT FOR 1897.

This report was as follows :-Infirmary : During the year 1897, 526 patients were treated in the infirmary an Increase of 92 over the number treated in the previous year. Of these 530 were males, and 176 females. The surgical cases numbered 439, including 235 accidents. The medical cases numbered 87. Of the accidents 84 were fractures. 'fractures of the leg 58, thigh 15, skull 4, ribs 4, other bones 5. The average number of beds occupied was 34. During the year, 30 deaths occurred in the institution, 20 from disease and 10 from injury. An increased number of patients were sent to the conva- lescent hospitals. To the Barnes Convalescent Home Cheadle 2, Devonshire Hospital, Buxton 2, Convalescent Hospital,Soutbport 9,Children's Sanatorium,Southport 4. The following operations were performed during the year :-Amputation of thigh 1, leg 2, foot 2, hand 1 ; abdominal section tor appendicitis 2, obstruction 1 ; ab- ecese of liver, incision, 1, empyema, incision, 2, excision of hip 9, knee 1, ankle 1; herniotomy 4, hernia, radical cure 2, miscellaneous minor'sperations 38, osteotomy 2, ovariotomv 1, removal of breast for cancer 1, post-nasal adenoids epithelioma 2, testis for sarcoma 1, jaw for sarcoma 1, simple tumours 4, ttremerrhoids 1, diseased bone 11, ganglion of wrist 1; tracheotomy 2, transfusion 4, trephining 1. Dispensary : During the year 1897, 4,716 dispensary patients were treated. Of these 1,820 were accidents or emergency cases: 2,012 were medical and surgical out-patients; and 664 were patients treated at their own homes. In connection with the homE visit- ing 4,759 visits were paid. The following cases of frac- ture and dislocation were treated :-Eractures of the forearm 45, clavicle 28, scapula 1, humerus 12, leg 5, fingers 13. ribs 4,.nose 1; dislocation of the forearm 6, humerus 9, scapula 2, fingers?, toes 2. The Cumulus, in moving the adoption of the report and accounts, said it was a matter to be regretted that the donations received during the past year only amounted to £7l 6s 11d, as against £605 16s in the r re- ceding year. On the other hand their expenditure was increasing owing to the larger number of patients. He was sure the paragraph in the report referring to the death of Dr. T, Starkey Smith, and Mr. Thomas Morris, F.G.S, was one which would meet with their entire sympathy. With reference to the contributions from the workingmen it was very satisfactory to see that there was such a substantial and continuoas increase. Start- ing in 1876 with a donation of 12s. 61. it had risen to £5lB 83 2d., in 1895, and ECM 103 9d during the past year. (Hear, hear). That last named sum was the highest which had ever been contributed by the Workingmen's Committee:to the Infirmary, and brought up the total contributions from that source to , £7,769 18f. qd. (Applause.) He thought one satisfac- tory feature about this increase was that it showed that the workingmen of the town were alive to their respon- sibilities. It was very satisfactory to the Board of Man- agement that workingmen showed their appreciation of the institution by the handsome subscriptions they made from year to year. If they had a larger income the in- stitution could be made still more useful than it was. At present it did a splendid work in the town, and those who had to do with its management were quite satisfied as to the value of the institution to the inhabitants at large. The last paragraph of the report referred to the subscriptions received from the general public. It was only fair to state that the list of subscriptions had only increased during the last 45 years from £213 to £332. The donations received from the Warrington Dramatic Society including £lO5 in 1897 amounted in the aggre- gate to £795 13s. 51. (Hear, hear.) Most of that sum had gone to the endowment fund. The Hoo. Secretary reminded him that the late Mr. G. Artinstall's legacy of £5OO was not included in this year's list of legacies. Mr.G. DARIN seconded the adoption of the report and accounts, which were unanimously agreed to. ELECTION OF TREASURER. -

div.head: -TTIE FEITHERS HOTEL ARBITRATION.
div.p: -TTIE FEITHERS HOTEL ARBITRATION.
- Sir,—ln your report, List week, of the proceedings in this case there are sems points in which, I think, the general public are interested. May I briefly advert to them.? .

The first thing that strirck me as very remarkable was the tremendous difference between the vendor's claim and the value put spa it by the .professienal ex- perts engaged in this case. From Mr. Arthur Browne's statement it appears that in 1894 the whole property was valued at £3,000, but when negotiations for its purchase by the Corporation were entered into the value suddenly rose to memo. in 1898. Another point that struck me forcibly was the experts estimate of the profits made by the publicans. These prcrfits were assumed as 34 per cent or one third of the whole drawimrs. Where is there another trade in Warrington where such financial results are obtained ! Well may the drink makers and sellers desire to multiply and replenish the eiath with their wares. Another point brought out at the meeting was the weekly sales of fully licensed oublic-houses. These were .put down at £25 to £2B. N)w there are 87 of these houses he Warrington, and taking the lowest estimate of .125 weekly, by a simple calculation we arrive at the astounding conclusion that the sum of £113,100 is spent in the public houses every year. But this is not all. If we add the modest sums of £l,ooa a month or so for the takings of the beer houses and off license holders the Warrington drink bill may, without exaggeration, be put down at one hundred and twenty-six thousand pounds per annum ! These figures suggest many pain- ful thoughts,but the most painful one is that the greater part of this huge sum is taken from the hard earned and small wages of the working classes.—Yours truly, OBSERVER.

div.head: ,BRIDGE-SfRF.ET ARBITRATION.
div.p: THE ,BRIDGE-SfRF.ET ARBITRATION.

Sir,—As this case is subjudice it is not my intention to make any comments which can be construed into an attempt to prejudice the issue,but a remark or two anent some of the incidents of the hearing may not be without interest. To begin with, everybody is puzzled to under- stand why an important public question, in which all the ratepayers are interested, should have been heard anywhere else but at the Town Hall. On Tuesday the small room at the Lion :Hotel was crowded to excesstand although the umpire, counsel, arbitrators, and others appealed to Mr. A. Browne for his consent to adjourn the hearing to a larger and in every way more comfortable and more suitable building (viz., the Town Hall), this gentleman for some inscrutable reason obstinately re- fused. Another interesting and noteworthy fact was the appearance of Alderman Thomas Sutton, J.P., chairman of the Street Improvement Committee, chairman of the Health Committee, Ice., in support of the claim of Mr. Arthur Wilson, and in opposition to the interests of the Corporation. It will be remem- bered that a few weeks ago Mr. Sutton attempted to disprove my statement that he was an " interested party" in regard to this Brldge-st, improvement, and he further gave your readers a very flattering description of his own disinterestedness wherever the interests of the Corporation were involved. If this present case is a fair example of the Alderman's zeal for the interests of his fellow-ratepayers we may well exclaim " Save us from our friends !" Let me further say that the initial steps in this important and costly improvement had to be taken by the Street Improvement Committee, of which Alderman Sutton is chairman. It is also worth noting that the figures relating to the pur- chase of other properties by the Corporation in Sankey-street and elsewhere, and, which were quoted so freely by Mr. Wilson's counsel, were in the handwriting of Mr. Alderman Sutton. and many of the properties were purchased at a time when the Alderman was himself a member of the Pro- perty Purchasing Committee. Need I say more? Yet another curious incident is the rumour persistently re- peated that a firm of brewers bad offered in writing a large sum of money for the Feathers Hotel, and that evidence to this effect would be put in. The facts proved to be that an offer had been made for the license alone, and that subject only to the consent of the magistrates to a transfer of the license to some other part of the town, and the amount offered for the license, altheal% not publicly disclosed, is now known. Mr. Taylor, counsel for Mr. Wilson, actually requested the umpire to permit Messrs. Walker's represen- tative to give his evidence as to this offer la camera, a request which was promptly and vigorously opposed by Mr. Bradbury, counsel for the Corporation, and as promptly refused by the umpire. Why in the name of all that is fair should such a request have been made ? Your readers will find much to interest them in the figures submitted by the valuers retained for Mr. Wilson, in their methods of arriving at their various estimates of the total valne of the property, and in the replies which Borne of them gave under the fire of Mr. Bradbury's persistent and vigorous cross-examination.— Yours, tee.,
STOCKTON HEATH ELECTION.

div.head: H. ROBERTS.
div.p: H. ROBERTS.

Sir,—The would-he autocrats of Stockton Heath are once more grieviously agitated at the prospects; of a poll. They seem to fight shy of polls. The seven champions of a caucus meeting have formed an alliance against all other cannidates for Parish Council honotirs,and have the assurance to ask the electors to return them in a body as the perfect Parish Council. Some of us, however, do not coincide with this opinion. Seven electoral addresses have been published and distributed (all in one envelope) to the electors ; tme purporting to come from each can- didate. They are not very promising epistles. Apart from their stereotyped character, the chief feature about them is their vapid and inconsistent statements ; and a persistent insistence about the demand for a poll. If we take these addresses as a criterion, we cr.uld not ex- pect much from their authors as a Parish Council. With your permission, Sir, I will quote a few extracts from them, and make a few comments. No. 1. This can hardly be termed an electoral address It is nothing but an artificial outcry about the cost of the poll (in capital letters). As a matter of course the other gentlemen re-echo the cry. Be says that at the Parish meeting, the choice of councillors was "clearly and unmistakably expressed." Now, Sir, any final decision, by show of hands. at a public meeting, can never be satisfactory. But when such a meeting is comprised mainly of partisans, and where the issues are the appointment of public representatives, then to expect minority candi- dates to abide by such decisions is unrelsonable and absurd. This demand for a poll is the keynote of each address ; ana what will this expensive poll cost after all? Very little more than what it must have cost these seven gentlemen to print and distribute the teat of their clamour. No. 2. This candidate's policy is "short," and part of it is "Lowest possible rates." Yet at the last parochial committee meeting he gave notice that at the next meeting he should move that the district surveyor's salary he increased. As this official is paid a salary from the Runcorn District Council, and as the Stockton Heath ratepayers contribute towards it, and also bearing in mind that £25 has already been added to his salary for extra work in Stockton Hath,l cannot reconcile this gentleman's action with his policy of " Lowest possible rates." . .

No. 3, "To the lighting, building, sewerage, fire, hydrants, sanitary matters,street forming, and building lines I have paid special attention." This is specific enough and no mistake: not a department of Parish Council work but what this gentleman is thoroughly acquainted with. But you know the adage "Jack of all trades master of none." In local matters I acknowledge no party ties. Now, surely the most dense of us cannot accept this, for has he not allowed himself to be in- cluded in " The seven" in this " local matter." No. 4. There is very little enthusiasm in this address. "I have been asked . . . . to which request I have, after careful consideration, acceded." What a gracious concession ! and how flattered we ought to feel. I dont want to, you know, but really as y3u are so pressing, etc., etc. "I offered to withdraw my candidature . . . . if that gentleman would withdraw also." How nice. Anything to oblige. "I am not aware that I have any fads. I may not have the opportunity of calling up- on you, tut I hope some of my friends will do so." Ne offence, I hope. The whole address has an air of dis- dain about it entirely out of keeping with what we ex- pect from a public representative. No. 5. Conspicuous like the rest for poll chatter and for the fact that his "strongest support for the welfare of the village" etc., is in smaller type than the rest of the address. Would the candidate doubting his abilities, have us pause before accepting this statement in its sincerity ? I have already occupied too much of your time and space, and will therefore bring my letter to an abrupt Conclusion.—Yours truly,
VIGILANT.

div.p: DRUNIOINNIIBB.

On Monday mO-reTicg—rt:.-t.t-i-e—Earlestown Police Station, before Mr. C. B. 11% Borron, Patrick Hanley, was charged on the information of P.C. Brindle with drunkenness. fhe ufficer mentioned, stated that the defendant was a collier hailing from St. Helens, and was found in an intoxicated condition on Saturday night in Earlestown. A fine of 53. and costs was imposed. Martin Rafferty, of Legh-street, Earlestown,was fined 23. 6.1. bud costs, for a similar offence. NEWTON DISTRICT COUNCIL.—TOWN HALL WARD

div.head: ELEcnox.
div.p: ELEcnox.

The election of a representative on the District Council for Town Hall ward takes place on Monday. The poll opens at 12 o'clock noon,the polling booths being at the Earlestown District school. Both can- didates (Mr. T. Robinson and Mr. W. Beatty) have during the week been well amongst the electors, and there is every indication that the fight will be an exceptionally stiff one.

div.head: EARLESTOWN ORCHESTBAL SOCIETY.
div.p: EARLESTOWN ORCHESTBAL SOCIETY.

Another, and the last, social gathering of the members of the above society took place on Satur- day evening in the Town Hall, Earlestown, and proved very enjoyable, a fairly numerous company being assembled. The proceedings which were much the same as those of previous gatherings of the kind, began shortly before 8 o'clock and termin- ated about 1/ o'clock, the Orchestral Society's band supplying the manic._

div.head: 'THE CLARION CYCLE CUM, NEWTON.
div.p: 'THE CLARION CYCLE CUM, NEWTON.

The recently formed cycle club in Newton, which is affiliated with the National "Clarion" Cycling Club has already secured a fair measure of success, and its membership roll is fully gratifying. Its secretary is Mr. H. Pearson, and the headquarters are at the Blue Bell hotel, Newton. At a meeting held on Monday night, the club decided to offer free membership to ladies. The captain (Mr. H. 'Ebben junior) also offers a prize value 10s. 61., to the member who attends the greatest number of club runs during the season. In other directions also the club is offering special advantages worthy the attention of intending members of both sexes. An excellent card of fixtures has been arranged, and some very enjoyable outings should result.

THE EARLESTOWN AND DISTRICT FANCIERS' CLUB. It will be remembered in connection with the re- cent meetings of this club, allegations were made against two members, Messrs. Widd and Dicliens, for some dealings in connection with a fowl sh)wn at the last exhibition. Mr. Widd laid the whole facts before the Poultry Club, and he has now re- ceived the following reply from Mr. H. T. Thornton, the hon. secretary :—" The matter of the complaint preferred against Mr. Dickens that he exhibited a borrowed bird at this show and against yourself in reference thereto, was considered by my committee at their meeting yesterday, when the following re- solution was passed. "The Committee after consi- dering the statements, are satisfied that the hen in question was the bona fide property of the exhibi- tor at the time of the show, and that no blame attaches to the Poultry Club representative, Mr. Widd, for not interfering in the matter." VIILCA.N WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.

In connection with the above school an illustrated concert was given in the schoolroom on Saturday evening. Songs and recitations were given by Misses M. Conway, It. Warburton, M. Ord, Messrs. Twemlow, C. Platt and James Huddleston. Bach item was illustrated by lime light views.the lantern being under the care of Mr. Lawson. In addition, "British bravery in Matabeleland," or " Major Wil- son's last stand" was also illustrated by the lantern, the connective narrative being read by Mr. Thomas Parr. The entertainment, which was in aid of the school funds, was of a most enjoyable and interest- ing character. On Sunday Mr. Thomas Parr con- ducted a very profitable gospel lantern service.

div.head: HOPE OF EARLICSTOWN LODGE, 1.0.G.T.
div.p: HOPE OF EARLICSTOWN LODGE, 1.0.G.T.

A good gathering was present at the Co-operative Hall on Monday evening. The chair was taken by the C.T. Bro. T. Cutler, and one candidate was ad- mitted to the lodge. The Secretary read a letter from the" Aehton Excelsior Lodge," and further discussions were held in reference to the " social." Bro. Roberta, of Warrington, reported that the "Temperance Mission," Warrington, had accipted the invitation visit to the lodge and will fulfil their visit next Monday night. Bro. J. Taylor gave the report of the visit to the Sutton Lodge, the meet- ing being afterwards thrown open. The programme for the evening was an "Essay Competition" in which five members competed. The meeting opened with an ode, followed by the competitors reading their papers. The judges after the reading of the papers retired to the ante-room, and on re-entering stated that Sister Coates of Haydock, and Bro. Barker of Eeriest° wn, were the winners, the first named being the winner of the firat prize. Bro. Woods then addressed the meeting on Sunday school work and juvenile templary work. Bro. J. Taylor said that all in the room had learnt some- thing from every one of the papers, and moved that the bes . thanks be tendered to the judges and the competitors. Thanks were then accorded to the judges who were Mr. Jring, Mr. Mullins, and Mr. G. Rawlins, and after responding the pleasant even- ing terminated. AMBULANCE COMPETITION' AT EARLBBTOWN. On Friday afternoon, the annual competition be- tween:ambulance teams, for the right of compet- ing in the general struggle for the possession of the challenge shield offered by the London and North Western Railway Company, took place in the Via- duct Institute, Earlestown. It will be remembered that when the shiell was first offered for competi- tion, two years ago, the honour of holding it for 12 months fell to the Viaduct Works team, but this year there was no team from the works. The com- peting teams on Friday were, Preston, Springs Branch, Wigan and St. Helens, five men comprising each team Dr. Handyside of Eeriest° wn was the examiner and he was assisted by Dr. Hayward of Haydock, and amongst others present were Mr. T. Ormand (chairman of the Wigan Centre), ani.Dlr. J. W, Emmett. The Secretary (Mr. Peters, station- master. Wigan) was unable to be present, but he sent a representative. Each team had five sets of first aid questions to deal with, each man taking one question,the question being affixed to the coats of five different boys, who acted as sub- jects. The questions were i—lat : Wound of palm of left hand with severe bleeding. Compound fracture of right knee cap com- municating with joints. 2nd. Bleeding from varicose vein of right leg. Fracture of o lecranon of left arm. 3rd. Incised wound on sole of left Coot with smart bleeding. Fracture of lower end of right armbone. 4th. Punctured wound a- back of left leg with severe arterial hemorrage.Fracture of right clavicle. 5. Wound with arterial bleeding in front of right elbow. Fracture of left thigh. The work performed by the men was not in any way up to the quality witnessed at previous competitions, there being too much book work, and too little practical work. The stretcher competition was severe scalp wound on back of head, compound fracture of right leg and arterial bleeding. The number of marks which could he gained by each time was 600, and the competition resulted as follows :—Preston 391, Springs Branch 307, Wigan 185, Sit. Helens 144. At the close, two members of the visiting team moved, and seconded a vote of thanks to Drs.ffandride and Hayward, which was put by Mr. Emmett, woo also en behalf of the directors expressed the thanks due to Dr. Handyside who had so ably conducted the examination, assisted by Dr. "ayward. Both the medical gentlemen suitably responded.

by the Council,—A letter, dated February 28th,was read From the Lancashire County Council,asking if the Council was willing to agree to the ordinary maintenance, repair and improvement of the main roads of the district for a period of one year from the 25th of March next, for a sum not exceedine £650, and for special works a sum not exceeding 275. It was resolved that the matter or the acceptance or otherwise of the offer of the Couoty Council be left in the hands of Mr. Berron, C.C., as also the qaestion of endeavouring to get the County Authority to make a grant fir the conversion of the boulders and setts betwen Evans and Co.'s coal yard and the Old Crow Inn, into macadam.—Tenders for the aewering of Athol and Albion streets were submitted, and it was resolved that th 3 tender of Mr. F. L. Bennie, of Warrington for the sowering (all labour and materials) of Athol-street for the sum of £2.11 33. and Albion-street £43 123. be accepted.—The Clerk reported the result of his interview with Mr. Worsley,with refer- ence to the power of the Council to collect tolls from mineral water manufacturers bringing goods into the district for sale, and stated that he had given it as his opinion that the Council could legally do so. A letter dated March 9th, 1898, was read from H. L. Riley, solici- tor, St. Helens, stating that he and hie clients did not take that view, and that he shotild advise them as to the best course to be adopted.—A letter dated March 10th was read from Messrs. R. Evans and Co., Limited, offer- ing to make that part of Clarence-street immediately ad- joining St. Helens-road, and which was to be MI feet wide, for the sum of £1.40, one-half of which sum (their proportion) they would pay on completion. It was re- solved that the offer be not entertained,and that Messrs. Evans and Co., be requested to make the street them- selves, in conjunction with that part facing their col- liery railway.—A letter, dated March 4th,was read from Mrs. Handyside complaining of the Council's workmen numbering the door ot the house without first asking permission. The matter was referred to the Chairman cf the Highway Committee. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT' BOARD AND TILE TOWNSHIPS SEWAGE DISPOSAL.

At a special meeting of the Highways and Sanitary Committee a letter was read from the Local Government B )ard adverting to a Local Government Board Inquire held by one of the Inspectors on the 18th January,ls9B, with reference to the application of the Council for sanction to borrow the sum of £15,000 for works of private street improvement stating that they could not sanc:ion the borrowing of the money by the Council un- til the Council had taken an adequate area of land for the purpose el' sewage disposal.—The committee resolved that the Assistant Surveyor be authorised to prepare a scheme of searage disposal on the lines adopted at Sal- ford and lay them before the committee at the earliest possible moment. Afterwards the Council might arrange that a deputation should wait upon the Local Govern- ment Board.—Plans for the mortuary were submitted, and it was resolved that subject to the approval of the Medical Officer of Hetlth and the substitution of glazed bricks the plans of the mortuary sdbmitted be adopted, and that it be erected in a suitable position near the Town Hall.—On the motion of MeCollingwood,seconded by the Chairman, the minutes were adopted. CONTEMPLATED IMPROVEMENTS AT THE RAILWAY S CATION.

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee the Clerk reported that from information which had been conveyed to him from a reliable source, he understood that owing to the correenondence which had taken place between him and the Railway Company with reference to the want of accommodation at Earlestown Station,the directors of th 3 company had decided to enlarge the platform on the North side of the station, increased waiting room accommodation to be provided, and a booking office to be erected on the sense side; separate means of egress and ingress will be provided. The company had also decided to erect a small booking office at the carve, and a porter would have instructions to attend there a sufficient time before the de;aartare of trains for the purpose of booking passengers. The Clerk further reported that he understood that the directors had given instructions to their engineer to devise a scheme, and prepare plans, for an underground passage from the station proper 0 the curve, to obviate the necessity of crossing the line, and when completed to submit the same to them for their consideration.—lt was resolved that the Clerk be directed to again communi- cate with the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany on the matter, and request that the work be pro- ceeded with as early as possible.—At a further meeting of the committee a letter was read from Mrs. Parry re- signing her position as part caretakor of the Town Hall. —The committee accepted the resignation.—The minutes were approved of. FINANCE COMMITTEE. - • -

Mr. Ormand,itie-Ch-ai-rm-ar-i ofthis committee moved the adoption of the minutes, which recommended that cheques be signed for the payment of the accounts of the fallowing ashpi's: general £1073 84 llitgas(revenue) £573 83 I, gas (loan) £B9l 10.3, water £BB 83 41., total £2428 153 91. The minutes also stated that the Collec- tor's statement of outstanding accounts for works of private street improvement in Mercer, Walrnsley,Birley, and Stanley-streets was submitted and it was resolved that the Collector again call upon the persons named for payment of the amounts set opposite their names, and if not so paid that they be served with notice to pay the same within seven days from the date thereof, and fail- ing compliance therewith that legal proceedings be taken for recovery of the amounts without further notice.— The Chairman of the Council and Chairmen of the Fin- ance and Highways Committees were appointed to consider the question of the Clerk's salary.— Mr. Gilmour called attention to an account of Doulton and Company, of St. Helens, for drain and sewer pipes and a ated that there was tie contract with Messrs. Doulton and Company. Ho thought people ought to know that they were not hound to have pipes from Doulton's.—Mr. Ormand said since the last 'fleeting he had spoken to several buililers with reference to these' pipes, and they told him that Doultorea were the best pipes that could bo obtained, and that in the great majority of cases they get them. They were not corn. pelled to have Daulton's. That was a misunderstanding of the Surveyor, and would be removed in the future. Fhey must, however,get a pipe equal to Doulton's which were first class pipes. He believed Doulton's were 11901 In 99 cases out of every 100, but he wanted it to be understood that no obligation reated upon them to pur- chase Doulten's.—Mr. Gilmour afterwards alluded to the fact that there was an account for £1 for literature. He thought the officials ought to buy their own literature. tie was also of opinion that £l2 was an unreasnat ably large amount to put down for Petty cash.—Mr. Ormand remieded the Council that Mr. Gilmour was a member of the Finance eommittee.and was a party to the accounts being Passed for payment. He came to-day an6l raised the question. How:was it he didn't raise it in Committee? All the ac- counts were there for his inspection. With reference to the points raised he might say that the payment for the " Urban District Council Surveyor" was agreed to by a special resolution of the Council, and it was not really a newspaper at all. With regard to the petty cash he(the3 Chairman of 'he committee) examined the beeka, and certified then' as biting correct. Tee district auditor in- sisted upon seeing a petty cash hook in which was re- corded every item of experiditure.—Tne Chairman said he was cure the Council had email leACe in the Chairman of the Finance Corn mitt e who went carefully into the matters affecting fiance.. With reference to tie petty cash accouut,the Chairman of tha committee went care- fully through the boake,and there could ho no reflacidon on the officials that anything WAS wrong in connection with them.—The minutes were then passed.
