div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICr COUSCIL.
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICr COUSCIL.

A meeting. -if this Council was held in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Monday afternoon. There were present Mr. C. B. F. Borron, J.P., C.C. (chairman), Messrs. W. Collingwood, (vice-chairman), J. W. Emmett, J.P., P. McMahon, W. Gilmour, F. J. Wood, R. Stone. J.P., t. Simpson, Dr. Patterson, W. Thompson, Rev. R. W. W. Kaye, J. H. Forster, E. T. Evans, T. Ormand, with Mr. W. W. Shirley (clerk), Mr. Brierley (surveyor), and Mr. Bowes (assistant surveyor). THE CHAIRMAN AND THE COUNCIL'S WORK.

The Ch-airman said that was the last meeting of the Council during their term of office, and personally he wished to thank the members tor their attention to the work of the Council and especially the individual chair- men of committees who had carried on their various work during the past year. He considered that good work had been done, lie was pleased to see that so many of the old members had retained their position as membnrs of the Council, but at the same time he re- gretted that they would lose their Chairman of the Cemetery Committee. No doubt the experience that the Rev. Mr. Kaye had obtained on the Council would be of service to him in the new district he is now residing in. THE VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES TO LORD .0 ERARD.. _

Mr. Gilmour asked if he would be in order if he named a subject which had previously been mentioned. Mr. Wood promised to get some information as to whether the Prince of Wales would come to Newton Bridge Station. He noticed that the doctor was getting his soldiers ready for the visit. He thought that as a loyal people theyin that district ought to give the Prince of Wales a loyal reception.—Mr. Wood : I will ease Mr. Gilmour's mind on the subject. I was told yesterday by Lord Gerard that the Prince of Wales was going to alight at Newton Bridge Station.—Mr. Gilmour: Ido think after the infoimation Mr. Wood has given us that we as a Council should show our loyalty and present an address to his Royal Highness at Newton Bridge. Mr. Ormond : I think we should first ascertain whether the Prince of Wales is prepared to accept an address.—The Chairman : I think that as Mr. Wood has been good enough to ascertain certain facts we may leave it to him to suggest what we should dc.—Mr. McMahon : We should be very much obliged if he would invite us to Garswood Hall. (Laughter.)—Mr. Wood : It is a strictly private visit,and whether an address would be acceptable I don't know.—Mr. Gilmour : It was stated in the Southport Council that it was to be a private visit,but the Council decided to present an address. It would not be refused. He (Mr. Gilmour) felt certain that it would be an honour to the district, and he thought it would bei a disgrace if something of the sort were not done at Newton,—Mr. Wood : As far as get- ting information goes I shall be pleased to get it for the Council,but I cannot promise to do more.—The Chair- man : I have no doubt we shall all meet the Prince with enthusiasm and do what we can to show our estimation of his services to the rionntry. (Hear, hear.)—The sub- ject then dropped. THE CEMETERY.

The Rev. E. W. W. Kaye moved the adoption of the minutes of the Cemetery Committee which stated that want of sanitary conveniences at the Cemetery was re- ported, whereupon it was resolved that the Chairman with the Surveyor and the Cemetery Kseper consider and recommend to this committee, which in their opin- ion is the best position in the Cemetery for the erection of sanitary conveniences, and that plans of the same with an estimate of the cost thereof be prepared by the Surveyor and submitted. The minutes were adopted. GAS AND WATER COMM' fEE—TEIE MANAGER'S

div.head: REPORT.
div.p: REPORT.

The Manager (Mr. Swann) reperted that the new steam boiler would very soon be ready for work, but it would be as well before it was put in use to have it caated with a non-conducting material. There would also be wanted a small steam-pump to connect up to the 2iin. cheek-feed valve, for getting into the boiler. They had now lying at the works the small steam-boiler (now out of use), and the remains of the old arnmoniacal liquor tank, and a few tone of cast iron, and ai cwt of old brass. He should therefore be much obliged if the committee would sell the whole lot, as it was taking up room of which they had vary little to spare. There was also about 23 tone of sulphate of ammonia in stock, and a large quantity of coke, which both should now be sold at the best price, as it wee costing too much for labour to trim and stock it up.—Mr. E i Bunting was building new property in St. John's-street and as there is no water main within about 90 yards of the same, you will therefore please give permission for the pipes to be laid. There is in stock as many 3 inch caet iron pipes as will be regaired for the job.—The hydrants have been ex- amined and tested, and are in good working order.—The consumption of water during the last four weeks,as per registering of the station meters, is as follows:—Viaduct Works meter, 3,250,000 gallons ; Newton Bridge meter, 1,550,000 gallons; Parkside meter, 11,000 gallons; total 4,811,000 gallons. Corresponding month lest year, 5,452,000 gallons ; den-ease, 611,000 gallons.— be Gas and Water Committee ordered that the new steam boiler at the GAS Works be coated with a non- cenducting material ; that the Clerk obtain tenders for the scrap iron and scrap brass at the (les Works ; that the Clerk obtain tenders for the 23 tons of sulphate of ammonia and sell at the hest pEce obtainable ; that the Clerk advertise in the local papers coke for sale at the Gat Works at the rate of 41. 6J. per ton, with special terms for a lame quantity ; that the Water Manager be instructed to extend the mating water main in St.John- et. to connect the heuse.s now being built by Mr. Bunting. It was also resolved by the Committee that the tender of Messrs. Cockrane and Co., of Woodside, near Dudley, far an estimated quantity of 14 tons 9 cwt;. of 16 and 18 inches cast iron pipais, for connecting the new puri- fiers to the new station meter, at the rate of £4 154. per ton, and 7 tons of special pipes at the rate of £9 10s. per ton be accepted.—Tee Chairman stated that it was very essential that the whole of the contemplated extensions at the Gas Works should be proceeded with with greater despatch than up to the present had been the case, otherwise he was afraid the Committee would be unable to cope with the increaced consumption of gas during the nest winter. div.head: EDUCATION CRISIS AT EA RLEST 0 W.N.
div.p: THE EDUCATION CRISIS AT EA RLEST 0 W.N.

To protest against the sectarian basis of the pro- posed new voluntary school at Earlestown, a meeting I was held in the Town Hall on Tuesday evening.called by the Local branch of the Northern Counties Education League. There was a good attendance of the public, and the meeting was presided over by the R3V. F. E. Miller, president of the branch,supported by the Revs.J. Allatt, P. R. Pasamore, Dr. Latham, S. Harvey, J. H. Profit, and Rev. ,T. Hirst Hollowell, of Oldham. The Chairman said they would remember that coins three months ago a meeting was held in that hall for the purpose of forming a branch of the Northern Counties Education League. As a coincidence that meeting was held at a time when the sluggish authorities under notice from the Education Board awoke to find that they should do something to a ards providing school accommo- dation in Eariestown. The committee who took the matter in hand for providing the school accommodation had been so active that they were still engaged in the preliminaries. (Laughter.) That meeting now found themselves face to face with what they anticipated at the beginning. The agitation for a voluntary school was not carried on for promoting education, nor in the Interests of children, but in the interests of the property owners, and the Established Church. There were many people who hoped that a voluntary school would be formed on lines that would be acceptable to all, and carried on in a way that would not be offensive to the parents of the children who would a, tend the school. He then read a circular,which had been issued to the largest ratepayers and to which was attached a description of the proposed school ex- tension scheme which was as follows :—" A grant of land from Lord Newton to the Rector of Newton-in- edakertield, situated near Newton Common, to hold the same unto and to the use of the said Rector and his suc- cessors, upon trust, to permit the said premises and all buildings thereon to be erected, to be for ever hereafter appropriated and used as a public elementary school." The management of this school shall be first vested in a committee, consisting of Lord Newton, or his nominee, and the Rector for the time being of the pariah of Newtonlo-Makerfield, and seven other persons to be nominated by the seven largest ratepayers, paying their full proportion of the building rate of Is. 31; and such representatives shall each pay to the funds of the school an annual subscription of,at least, 21s. during the term of their office. In Case any one of the seven largest rate- payer. fails to nominate a manager, then the committee shall accept the nominee of the next largest ratepayer who shall have previously paid the is. 3d.rate,to fill the vacancy. In case of death or resignation of their repre- sentative such ratepayer shall have the right to nominate a successor for the remainder of the unexpired term of three years. The control and management of such school and premises, and of the funds and endow- ments thereof, end the selection, appointment, aid dis- missal of the Schoolmaster and Schoulmistress, who shall be members of the Ceurch of England) and their assist- ants shall be vested in and exercised by the Committee of danagement, and the religious instruction shall at all times be conducted daily, according to the syllabus issued by the Diocesan Board of Education, and the pro- gress of the scholars therein shall be reported upon by the Diocesan Inspector, and no book shall be used for the purpose besides the Holy Bible, the Book of Com- mon Prayer, and such hymn book as may be approved of. ke, to, That meeting was called to protest against the sec- tarian basis of that new school. They did not meet in any hostility to education, or the London and North Western Company, and the large ratepayers, but they had met in hostility to the clerical party which was try- ing to work this meeting in its own interest. The site was to be given by Lord Newton. A landlord ought to regard himself so much the owner of his land, as the trustee of the public generally, They ought to put to Lord Newton this point, that his income was divided largely from land rents, paid by the people who lived upon his land. They found that the money by which the school was to be built would be made up, it was hoped by subscriptions from large ratepavere,bue those I large ratepayers were not the owners of the money. It belonged to the shareholders, and they had the right to say how it should be spent, (Rear, hear.) The tax- payer would have to keep the school going. They wanted a school which should provide religious instruc- tion that should be acceptable to all; a school that should not be controlled by a peer' a rector, and nominees of the largest ratepayers. They did well to protest against this scheme and try to bring what pres- sure might be brought upon Lord Newton, and to secure justice generally. (Applause.) The Rev. J. Hirst Hollowell said the struggle for popular control in which they were engaged was going on over the length and breadth of the land. He ven- tured to predict that at the next general election, apart from foreign politics, the great question before the electors would be "are the day schools of England which children are forced to attend, and which their fathers are forced to support, to be ruled by the people or the priests." Religious liberty was dear to the people of England. What would the men of Earlestown say if they were to be told that next Sunday they were to be compelled to attend a Wesleyan, Baptist or Congrega- tional place of worship ? It was not a question of what would be said, butwhat would be done. What right had they to compel the children of those parents to go to sectarian institutions five days out of each week ? If it was wroag to compel a strong man, it was worse to compel a weak helpless child. What was the com- pulsion in Newton-in-dfakerfield. He found seven day schools for the whole district of Newtcn-in-Makerfield, and six out of those were either Church of England or Cnurch of Rome. Out of the entire seven schools there was not one which was undenominational in manage- ment and sin out of the seven were either Anglican or Roman in their teaching. ('Shame.") What would the Church of England say if six out of those seven schools were Baptists, and nothing but Baptist tenets were taught. Sectarian education was third class education. That had been proved. Sr John Gout said educatii,n- ally the rural districts were behind Denmark. Who had control of the rural districts ? The clerical party. The education of the rural districts had been Sectarian edu- cation. On the average, es,hools which had been built by the people at their expense,and,under their management had better buildings, better playgrounds, better staffs, better pay,and a staff which possessed the indispensable requisite,liberty of conscience. When they deprived the teacher of liberty of canscience,they degraded the teach- ing. The proper thing to do was to set up a School Board, but in order to keep the people quiet a promise was made that something of the nature of an unsectarian school was going to be Set up. Such an impression was produced, but a hope was held out that the new school which was going to be built would not be unpleasant to Non-conformists. That was to keep them quiet. That game had been played before and one was always pre- pared fox it. The fact of the matter was the Church of England did. not believe in unseotarian education. What 'it did believe in was making all classes, and all denom- inations pay the cost of sectarian education. An muse- tarian school was a national school. A. sectarian school was not a national school in any sense, except that the nation had to pay for it. This promise that they should have an unsectarian achool was worth just about as much as that which the Turkish Government gave, that there should be reform in their provinces. The scheme, as explained by the Chairman, was in accordance with the old Tory clerical period. That meeting was going in for the largest number of ratepayers however poor they might be, and there was never a greater insult to the Christianity of this com- munity than that the 7 largest ratepayers should manage the school. (Applause.) Somo people were the largest ratepayers as soon as they were born, they could I not help it. No schoolmaster or schoolmistress was to be appoiated unless a member of the Church of England. That was an infamy. If they were men they would rice up against this tyranny, and would never cease un- til they had schools under popular control in Earlestown (Applause.)

• The Rev. P. R. Passmore moved " That this meeting having had laid before it the proposed constitution of the new Elementary School at Earlestown, emphatically condemns the provisions contained therein on the grounds : First, that grave injustice was to be inflicted on the Non-conformist population of the township by the use of the prayer book, and the placing the religious in- streintion and the general conduct of the school under the control of representatives of the Established Church; second, that the provision that the scboolmastAr and schoolmistress must be members of the Church of England imposes a cruel religious disaleility on many of the most honourable and competent of the teaching pro- fession ; third, that grave wrong will be done to the Non-Conformist shareholders of the subscribing com- panies by the use of their money to provide for inculcat- ing tenets of which they disapprove." Mr. J..l3..Profit seconded. _

-Dir. W. Gilmour said,as a member of the Urban Dis- trict Council ha would ranch rather have a Board school man a denominational school. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was then put and unanhnously car- ried. _

The Rev. James Allett, in moving a vote of thanks to the Rev. J. H. Hollowell, for his address, also spoke against the proposed sectarian basis of the school. Dr.Lathain seconded.and sai-1 he had recsived a letter ' from the Hon. T. W. Legh,M.P., in which he said " I am not aware whether the committee to which you re- fer was representative or not of the various denomina- tions. If it was it seems to me that you can scarcely complain of its recommendations." From Mr. Squires of the firm of Evans and Co., Haydocit, he had received the following : " I have your letter of the 19do March iegardin. proposed new school at Esrlestown. This is tide first I have heard of the matter. I shall certainly advocate the views you support in your letter." That was very encouraging. fie thought they could safely say that solar as that company was concerned, they would not contribute to that diabolical scheme. The motion was carried, and the meeting afterwards dispersed.

THE LIST MEETING OF THE BOARD.

A meeting of the Board of Guardians—the last of the present term of office—was held in the Board Room at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr. G. Pilling presided,and there were also present: —Mrs. Clay, the Rev, T. R. Matthews,Dr.Patterson, Messrs. J. W. Knowles, William Houghton, 5. P., A. Jolley, A. J. Jolley. S. Davies, William Hickman, G. div.p: AR INMATE'S COMPLAINT.

The Local Government Board forwarded a copy of a letter thes had received from Mr. Keefe, one of the mates, complaining of the action of the Matron in de- priving him of some uaderclothing which he had been accustomed to wear.—lt was decided to refer the matter t 3 the House Committee. _ THE VACCINATION OF CHILDREN. _ _

—.----- The Local Government Board wrote :siring for a stricter carrying out of the Vaccination Act in Mr. Hob- son's district—Mr. Clarke said there were some places in the country where the Act was hardly carried out at all. In Nelson for instance there were thousands of unvac- cinated children. It was a well-known fact that 21. a case was given by the authority, and the year's salary did not amount to LIT. Ho thought it was ridiculous for the Local Government Board to complain of districts where it was practically attended to.— Me Chairman: We are simply working under the instructions of the Local Government tioard.—Mr. Clarke: They make a mark of one place.—The subject then dropped. APPOINTMENT OF A SUPERINTENDENT NURSE. _

The House Demmittee attar considering the applica- tions for the position of superintendent nurse ordered that the following candidates be requested to attend the Board meeting :—Ellen Itingrose,of the InfirmamOtter- shaw, Chertsey; Agnes Gibb Sleven,of the South Eastern Hospital, New Cross-road, London ; and Jane Jeffery, of the Workhouse Infirmary, Newton Abbot, South Devon. —Miss Ringrose did not appear,but the other two ladies mentioned appeared before the Board.—Mr. Hickman afterwards moved that Miss Jeffery be appointed to the position.—Mrs. Clay secouded, and the resolution was unanimously passed.—Miss Jeffery was then called into the room and informed of the decision of Van Board. It was declded that she should commence her duties six weeks hence.

div.head: LADIES' VISITING COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE LADIES' VISITING COMMITTEE.

Mrs. James Fairclough wrote stating that the Ladies' Visiting Committee were desirous of giving a tea and entertainment to the inmates of the Workhouse if the Guardians had no objections to their doing so. If the Guardians assented to the proposal they suggested Thursday, the 28th April, as the date. They would be much pleased if any member of the Board would come to the entertainrnent.—Mr. Thompson moved that the kind offer of the Ladies' Committee be accepted.—Mr. Bibbert seconded the proposition, which wne carried.

lir.—B-L-L-fie—oi-referred to the fact that it was no last special meeting of the Board, and he thought a vote of thanks was doe to the Chairman. He paid a tribute to the distinguished services of Mr. Pilling during his term of office as Chairman of the Board,end also to his services as Chairman of the Assessment Committee. He felt surd that the Board would he unanimous in tendering their warmest thanks to Alr.Pilling for his services. lie there- fore had pleasure in moving a vote of thanks, and he hoped Mr. Pilling would be re-elected a member of the Board at the forthcoming election.—Mr. A. J. Jolley seconded the vote of thanks. He thought they would all be unanimous in expressing their esteem,and hoping that they would have Mr. ?Ming amongst them again after the election. It was a matter of common notoriety that he was opposed because he was Chairman of the Assessment Committee, whose actions had beisn exposed to considerable adverse criticism during the past six moeths. Some of the people apparently who were be- hind Mr.Pilling's opponent seemed to have entered upon a campaign of misrepresentation which was to be re- grated. He did not wish to say one word against the gentleman coming out against Mr. Pilling. No doubt he was a straightforward and honourable professional gentleman, and he did not wish to cast any doubt on the right of any man to fight any seat he thought fit. But when a men had given so largely of his time, energy, and ability to the public service it deserved some recognition, and he thought it might have been recognised by Mr. Pilling being spared the trouble and expense of a contested election. That was not the time or plane to review the action of the Assessment Committee, but with regard to the question at issue he might be permitted to remark that there had been a good deal of mis-representation in the press and on placards. He understood that there was to be a meeting fa support of Mr. Pilling's opponent that night,and it was quite possible that these mis-re- presentations might be repeated and unfortunately some people might be misled. That was the reason why he wished to say a word about it now. It seemed to him that the real point in connection with the action of the Assessment Committee was being obscured,whether con- sciously or not it was not for him to say. But it was legitimate f n. him to sly that the point to be considered and which the Assessment Committee had considered in assessing licensed houses in the Union, was that the committee had not taken into consideration the license, nor the business that was done, nor the capital value of the premises, but simply the anneal value of the hoes-% Th t h-ld been laid down by the highest courts. PI wool! he preposterous for the Assessment Committee to yield to the ignorant clamour and depart from'a judicial attitude and attempt to alter the adminis tration of ties law. It was a mistake to attempt to put publicans deliberately down as ruemb-re of the criminal classes. It seemed to be suggested that some!' aw Mr. Filling aid the Assessment Committee had leaned in favour of the brewing interests. If anyone would get up and publicly make that statement, one would be able to meet the etatement. It was diffieult to meet insinua- tions'. But he did say, and he thought all his colleagues would endorsr it, that any such insinuations against the committee or the chairman were without foun- dation. (Naar, hear). No man could act • more fairly in the c%sir than Mr. Pilling had done, and to have Imparted into the assess- ment q ee‘tion sentimental considerations was entirely wrong. The point at issue was a legal and technical one, and ought to be discussed In a calm cud) die's! spirit. It was not a eubject to be debated noun plat- forms or to be settled by placards on the walls or by one- sided statements in the press. Be thought he should only he re-echoing the sentimeee of the Board when he said that th-v hoped Mr. Pilling would be returned again —Mr. William Houghton characterised the opposi- tion to Mr. Pilling in Plirfi•li Ward as on- worth, and unwarrantable.—Mr S. D ivies said no one wee more surprisei than himself al- ter the honourable arra ngemen 's made by all concer ,pd, that Mr. Pilling and other members of the Board were put to tho trouble of a contest and to an unnecessary expens.. Re was inclined to think there had been a very mischievous spirit abroed, and he felt that the opposition to the chairman wasn't really seri- ous, because above all men a doctor with a private prac- tice could not possibly attend to the duties reel sired of him on this Board. They had one doctor on the B eird who had said that his private practice 'had interferred with his attendance on the Board. D nters were better attending t their own business than to the tittles of the Board. (Laughter.) div.head: AND MR. THOMPSON.
div.p: AND MR. THOMPSON.

Mr. A. J. JOLLRY proposed a vote of thanks to the Ladies' Committee. He said that during the past these years the members of the Ladies' Committee hal gives a large amount of time to tho work they hid in hand, and had initiated oertain reforms.—Mr. Hickman seconded,and tho vote was unanimously agreed to.—Mrs. Clay rlspended on behalf of the Ladies' Coinmitte.—Mr. Hickman said as they had now farmed themselves into a mutual admiration society he would like to mention that they were losing the services of Mr. Thompson and he was sure they all felt that they were losing the ser- vices of a very valuable guardian. He beloved he was voicing the feeling of every member 'of the Board and every official of the Union when he said how very sorry they were that the state of Mr. Thompson's health bad compelled him to withdraw from the valuable work he had taken such an active part in during the past three or four years. He had rendered valuable service, and his kindly sympathy towards inmates had been expressed on many I occasions, and notably in the getting up of entertain.. meats for their benefit. He wished Mr. Thompson could have seen his way to come back again. He was sure Mr. Thernpson had the sympathy of the Board, and every member hoped that his health would be permanently restored. He had pleasure in proposing a vote of thank, to him for his services.—Mr. Houghton seconded, and Mr. A. J. Jolley, the Chairman, Mrs. Clay, and Mr. Malkin supported. The motion was unanimously passed. —Mr. Thompson responded, and said it had been a pleasure to him whilst he had been a member of the Board to find employment for a number of inmates, and give them a helping hand. He was always glad when he could give a man a start if he was willing to work. This concluded the business.

NOCICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for S COUNTY OF CHES E'ER will be held at the COURT KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on alosina.v, the 4th day of April next, at half-past eleven h'elock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be eraDannelled. .The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds °.0.1 Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the ."'ltsford District, and the trials of all prisoners cam- nutted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Bersioeg The Grand and Petty Juries for the liEnutsford bistrict.must be in attendance at the Court House, Xnutsford at the opening of toe Court on MONDAY, the 4th day of April next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the I?°roution. The COURT will be Adjourned to the Castle of Chester. on THURSDAY, the 7th day of April next, at eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTION NEWTON IN MAKIDIFIELD, TO THE ELEC- TORS OF THE TOWN HALL WARD. LADIES AIM GENTLE/LIM, Having been requested to allow myself to be nominated as a Candidate for a Seat on the District Couno at tke forth- coming election and having consented to cie so, beg leave to plane my services at your disposal. I am in favour of a stringent administration of Sanitary Laws particularly with respect to the proper and efficient sewering and paving of the many private streets, whish are at present far from being in a healthy condition and if elected I shall support any step, which may be taken whick will tend to remedy the present unsatisfactory condition of things as I hold sanitation to be the first and foremost duty that,,a Local Authority is called upon to perform. I am also In favour of the Urban District Council construct- ing their own Water Works so that they may be in a position to have the absolute sontrol of the Water supply of the dis- trict in their own bands. Whilst holding the view that the affairs of the Township should be conducted with strict economy, I shall always sup- port any reasonable expenditure which will tend to the better administration of the affairs of the district for the benefit of the Ratepayers at large, Should you honour me by electing me as your representa tive on the Council. I e LAI I endeavour to attend to the duties of the office to the best of my ability and te the beat interests of the district In general. I ant, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, NIAS ROBINSON. Market-street, Earl este wn, March 18th, 1898.

Jenkins was chairman and gave a brief address, his subject being " Books, Food for the Mind." In connection with this subject he made a very sympathetic reference to Mr. Gladstone's illness. The speaker for the afternoon was Mr.Stringer,of Manchester, who gave ,a very able address on the words" For none of us liveth to Himself." Mr. Thomas Johnson, of Rua- corn sang very efficiently " Why do the nations," and Messrs. Thomas and Reginald Johnson sang a duet "The lord is a Man of war" from Flandell's "Israel in Egypt," which was much appreciated. The Rev. John Yonge read the scripture lesson and Mr.T. Hawthorn offerea prayer. The lame number of prize books displayed in the church bad a very bright and attractive appearance, although the number distributed was not so large as in previous half years.
